prompt and generates a response from its learned parameters. It does so by predicting tokens one at a time. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">RAG: In RAG, the user query goes to a retriever before the LLM. The retriever fetches relevant information from the indexed knowledge base and passes it to the LLM along with the query. The LLM generates a grounded response, but it does not guarantee correctness. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">AI agent: It has a goal and keeps track of the current task state. It can plan about what to do next, call tools, get a result back, observe it, and repeat until the goal is met. This feedback loop allows the agent to observe the results and adjust its actions accordingly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Agentic AI: Putting one or more AI agents to meet a shared objective is what makes an AI system agentic. It is achieved through planning, tool use, and feedback. You add an orchestration layer, which coordinates work across multiple agents and workflows. Agents read and write to shared task states and can access tools, data, and the environment.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: calling are mechanisms that allow an LLM to have access to tools. The agent runtime sends the prompt to the LLM, the LLM decides which tool to use and emits a tool call request. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The agent runtime then handles tool call execution and returns the results back to the LLM to continue. The LLM finally produces a final output shown to the user.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What is different between the two is where the function is implemented, and how the agent handles the execution. In local function calling, the functions are implemented locally on the user's machine. The agent runtime executes them and receives the results.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In MCP, the functions can be outside of the user's machine, on some remote server. The agent runtime follows the MCP protocol and calls the corresponding server, the execution happens remotely, and the results are sent back to the agent runtime. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This allows your agent to connect to hundreds of thousands of tools that are implemented publicly and hosted remotely.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Over to you: What are the best MCP resources out there?</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px item.title: Measuring AI’s Impact On Delivery Speed
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Measuring AI’s Impact On Delivery Speed

James Shore

“Is AI making software development faster? Most people I talk to say “yes.” But how much? What value are you getting for your money? Are there other ways of using AI that have a better ROI?”

#Management Metrics AI
item.description: Measuring AI’s Impact On Delivery Speed

item.title: Expected Goals
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Expected Goals

Mike Fisher

“Write the hypothesis down before the result arrives. Not the goal, the reasoning. What you expect to happen, why you expect it, what would tell you that you were wrong, and what you knew at the time. It is the only way I know to stop your future self from rewriting your past self’s thinking to match whatever happened.“

#Management GoalSetting DecisionMaking
item.description: Expected Goals

item.title: Introducing CAFE(S): A Framework For Defining AI Context Quality
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Introducing CAFE(S): A Framework For Defining AI Context Quality

Brian Houck

CAFE(S) names five properties of good context. The first four ask whether the context lets agents do good work - clarity, actionability, fidelity and efficiency. The fifth - security - asks whether the context is safe to use at all.

#Strategy AI Agents
item.description: Introducing CAFE(S): A Framework For Defining AI Context Quality

item.title: Defensive Driving For Your Career
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Defensive Driving For Your Career

To have a positive career you need to be appropriately recognized and rewarded for your work. The author shares techniques to take credit for your work while “driving defensively.”

#Influence CareerGrowth
item.description: Defensive Driving For Your Career

item.title: My Development Setup In 2026
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
My Development Setup In 2026

Brandon Weaver

“As I start to step into another new adventure I took a long hard look at my development setup on my work laptop as well as my home laptop and realized I haven’t really cleaned it up in what, a decade now? It was time for some spring cleaning to get it under control and start asking hard questions about what added value and what had somehow smuggled its way across migrations over the past decade. This post explores some of my setup, why I made certain decisions, and how I’m different now than I was back then.”

#Tools+Setup
item.description: My Development Setup In 2026

item.title: How To Prepare For AI-Driven Code Modernization Projects
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How To Prepare For AI-Driven Code Modernization Projects

“This article covers the work enterprises must do before the modernization takes place: defining what done means, what evidence a change must carry, how certified changes will reach production, and what has to be staged so the run can start.“

#Architecture TechDebt AI
item.description: How To Prepare For AI-Driven Code Modernization Projects

item.title: The Test Suite Is The New Code Review
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Test Suite Is The New Code Review

Allen Hutchinson

“The fix I’ve settled on is structural. When a piece of functionality is clean enough to stand on its own, I pull it out into its own repository before it tangles into everything else. It gets its own tests, its own merge queue, its own release cadence. An agent working inside it can hold the whole thing in its head.”

#CodeReview AI Testing
item.description: The Test Suite Is The New Code Review

antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">1. Writing code by hand: is it over?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The creator of Ruby on Rails, David Heinemeier Hansson, caused quite a stir yesterday (Wednesday) with comments in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e4ced339-8d7b-40f7-aba8-38c0dffe50fe?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">his Rails World keynote</a><span>, when he revealed that coding by hand is dead at his company, 37signals.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is a big deal because 37signals created Ruby on Rails, and they are known for their software craft there, especially when it comes to code quality. It’s also a business that’s 27 years old and is profitable. Despite that pedigree, DHH caused a stir among the dev community, saying:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong>At 37signals, a couple of weeks ago, we made the decision that it clearly means we’re done writing code by hand.</strong><span> We have gone pencils down on the idea that we were gonna write code by hand, as a normal course of business creating things.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Writing code by hand at 37signals is now an exceptional state. It is like seeing a bug in Sentry: something here went wrong; why was the agent not able to produce what we wanted? Okay, maybe for a little while, we’ll still get the old pencil out and dot it down for them, but then we fix the machine, we fix the factory, we get things going again. This is a recognition of what’s already happening.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">DHH compared the maturation of AI tools into being highly capable at coding with the impact upon the craft of painting of the arrival of the camera:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“On November 24th, 2025, we got the “Kodak Brownie” of our era. We got Opus 4.5\. AI technology, accessible in a harness that many people could afford to use and experience for the first time what it’s like to create software in pairing with a new form of intelligence. This was the tipping point for me. There was everything before November 24th, and then there was everything after. This is going to be the date that history books going forward will mark as the inflection point for the age of agents.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">He shared how 37signals has embraced a future where coding by hand is almost entirely absent:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Embracing native mobile apps instead of web: </strong><span>famously, 37signals is bearish on native iOS and Android apps and has built web versions instead. With AI, they are betting on native apps being much easier to be built with a small team and are already building new ones.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Moving backend services to Rust, not Ruby</strong><span>: This is due to performance reasons and because agents write good enough Rust. That’s remarkable to hear from the creator of Ruby on Rails!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Ruby on Rails remains for web apps</strong><span>: 37signals is not leaving RoR behind, but only because Ruby on Rails’ convention-over-configuration design makes it easy for agents to work with it.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">DHH closed by revealing that he no longer even thinks of himself as a professional programmer (emphasis mine):</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“I have retired from being a professional programmer. I think it was somewhere around 4 to 5 months ago, maybe March. I spent a quarter of a damn century chiseling code by hand and loving every moment of it. This is not something to look back upon with regret; this is something to look back upon with joy and accept that it is over.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Writing code by hand is no longer an economically productive enterprise for the vast majority of programmers working at the vast majority of companies</strong><span>. On the other side of that is a new career as a professional maker of things, steering intelligence that was only available in science fiction up until a few moments ago.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One of the things we’re gonna have to revisit is everything we think we know about software architecture. The main tool that we’ve used for a very long time is abstractions. Abstractions don’t make quite the same sense in the age of agents. The reason we did abstractions was in part not to repeat ourselves; well, now the price of repetition has gone to near zero.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s worth noting DHH’s keynote chose a spicy topic for a conference attended by engineers who are personally and professionally invested in the craft of building software!</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">Decline of coding by hand is long predicted</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the first issue in The Pragmatic Engineer this year, on 6 January, I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/15ae9753-cc5a-490f-b251-a7383b841c2e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">wrote</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong>When AI writes almost all code, what happens to software engineering?</strong><span> No longer a hypothetical question, this is a mega-trend set to hit the tech industry. (...)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The bad news is that change will probably be rapid. It’s barely been a year since the idea of Claude Code was born in Boris Cherny’s head, and already similar tools like OpenCode, Codex, Factory, Amp, Cursor, and more capable agents are changing how software is written. Change has always been part of working in tech, but I cannot recall it being this fast, or happening across the whole industry at once!”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I concluded that this change was on its way, based on my own experience of building software with Opus-4.6 and GPT-5.2, and from talking with experienced engineers who had resisted “AI hype” for good reason, but who had come to see that AI can now generate code that’s “good enough” in many cases.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Back then, I made a few predictions about what will happen when AI agents are producing most of the code for engineers:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Sloppier code</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Weak software engineering practices hurting sooner</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">“Coders” who are not software engineers see less demand</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Tougher work-life balance for engineers</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Junior engineers pushed to become seniors, fast</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Computer science education increasingly required for new hires</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">A massive explosion in code and software, for which someone must be accountable</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So far, it’s a messy transition and we engineers are responsible and accountable for a lot more code that we didn’t write, but which is in production anyway.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">Non-engineers also getting into agents</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the end of January, I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/11430278-f14b-495f-bd71-12cc4173a162?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">shared a deepdive</a><span> that was pretty close to home for me: my brother’s 30-person, 15-engineer startup, Craft Docs, made its own sharp pivot to AI by building their own AI harness for non-engineers – called Craft Agents – two weeks before Claude Cowork was released, and months before ChatGPT Work launched.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Craft resisted the temptation to use AI when it did not feel productive, but with the model releases of November 2025, they found LLMs are not only useful for coding, but also for non-engineering work like customer support. In the deepdive, I went into more detail about non-engineering use cases (which engineers enabled) like:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Automatic triaging of bug reports with agents</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Data enrichments added to all workflows</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Customer support “skills” like processing feature requests</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The marketing team building websites without devs</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">HR automating tedious work</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Finance automating personal workflows</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Craft Docs seemed early to a trend that has become more widespread, by having both their own engineering and non-engineering folks onboard to an AI harness. Now, there are signs other companies are doing the same: at OpenAI, non-engineering units like finance, recruitment, and legal moved over to Codex in June 2026:</p><div An engineer with the username voxium </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce85fe9d-4742-4477-bcc0-5243330827ec?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">posted</a><span> (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“The state of engineering right now is horrible. It has been half a month since I started a new role at a big company.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Nobody knows anything here. The specs, code, tests, PRDs, tickets, resolution of those tickets, reports, etc., everything is made by Claude Code. Nobody on my team likes this.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They are being forced to ship as much as they can. I have heard multiple times from higher management that pushing code is not a bottleneck, so why are we slow?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">People are working 12 to 13 hours a day just to press enter. Nobody is reading anything. Humans in corporate are doing nothing on their own.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Everyone, literally everyone, from an L1 to an L7 engineer here is doing the same thing. Talk to Claude.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>There is no sense of victory. Nobody is resolving bugs. In reality, nobody is thinking anymore.</strong><span> Everything is done by LLMs. It is so soul-sucking.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I would not mind it, to be honest, if we were at least given the time to check out the code and see what is going where. But no, the goal is to just ship. No matter what happens.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This post rings true because it </span><em>is</em><span> happening at many places where there’s more AI usage, engineers do “outsource” thinking to LLMs, and end up not caring about anything else except shipping </span><em>something</em><span> to production.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">Quality in decline</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since the beginning of the year, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/672999b9-b9e8-4c7c-84c9-c5768a5e6abf?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">the quality of software has been degrading</a><span> pretty much everywhere, much of it caused by over-reliance on AI, or perhaps more accurately, the outsourcing of thinking and decision making to AI. In July, I moved my video podcast off of Spotify after a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d5f608b0-b3e3-42ea-9e20-494b2fc1ba7e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">series of unexplainable outages</a><span>, and Spotify’s engineering team seemed to take no real pride or accountability in fixing the root causes of the issue.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Only this week, Uber shipped a new feature to production in the Uber Eats app – a new way to select extras with your food order – with seemingly no QA testing:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table Can you spot two obvious, sloppy bugs on this page?</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Inside this new “add-ons selector” in Uber Eats, I noticed three bugs at once:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>“Choose up to 999”</strong><span>: no engineer, designer, or PM bothered to check what happens when a restaurant does not fill out a number on how many toppings to add, or adds a ridiculously large number. The most toppings that my screen allowed to be selected was six and not 999, so I could not even choose the option of 999 buns for my burger.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Sloppy overflow. </strong><span>A rule of thumb, during my time at Uber, was that text will never overflow, even when localized. Basilcummaynaise (basil mayo in Dutch) broke this rule but still shipped.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Functional bugs in the selector. </strong><span>I originally tried to order from my favorite Mexican place: a bowl with no rice or bulgur as the base. There’s the option to select “rice”, “bulgur” or “nothing” as the base, but selecting “nothing” counts as an extra side, and the app doesn’t allow the ordering of a bowl with no base.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’ve used the Uber Eats app for years, and this was the first time I saw such a sloppy feature release. I assume that devs and PMs building it have all “checked out”, stopped doing proper QA, and assume that the agent will take care of all of it. There’s no other way to explain three bugs shipped to all customers but seemingly noticed by nobody until I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/52b084b3-3831-4486-b6d7-e49db5ba0372?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">posted</a><span> about it. </span><em>To the Uber Eats team’s credit, they reached out and are looking into fixing all three issues.</em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">Software engineering to be more important than ever</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’m personally past the shock and grief stages of agents taking over the activity of coding. At first, I assumed this change would reduce the amount of work for engineers. But, counter-intuitively, that actually seems to be growing:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>We need to understand the characteristics of LLMs better. </strong><span>LLMs feel familiar as they can produce text in a way only humans could do before. But they are less reliable, still prone to hallucination, suffer from capability gaslighting, and many other problems. They can also be expensive and slow.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>New systems need to be engineered. </strong><span>Agentic “software factories” can now produce code, based on the input provided. But how is this code validated? How much can detecting defects or various issues be automated? This is a brand new area, and we need to build new types of systems, often based on old ideas. One such example is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2a789ea-1715-4243-89c0-11c365f59f8e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">OpenAI’s software factory</a><span>, the other one is Ramp’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/924af6f3-eaa1-4818-b6ce-5dd5b427a405?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Inspect internal coding harness.</a></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Nondeterministic LLMs can generate deterministic code. </strong><span>An area I feel is under-explored and under-appreciated is the use of LLMs to substitute LLMs usage in agentic “software factories” with deterministic code they generate. For example: instead of running AI code review that is expensive and slow on all PR requests, could AI generate linters that catch the majority of common issues? If this is possible, complex lint rules would run faster, be more reliable and cheaper to execute than LLM calls.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>New categories of systems and products will be built by engineers who “get” LLMs and AI engineering. </strong><span>We are seeing the majority of venture funding pour into AI companies because AI creates new business models, new revenue streams, and disrupts “traditional” software. For example, who would have thought that companies would spend tens of thousands of dollars, per engineer, on AI coding tools? Or that the category of AI inference providers would become as massive as it already is from barely existing two years ago?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This technological change will re-jig parts of the tech industry: the winners will surely win big, and teams and companies choosing inaction could be out-executed and displaced by nimble competitors. And in many ways, this is great news for us software engineers who keep up with the technology. Companies are now investing in innovation and are willing to pay top-of-market for software engineers who can help them build AI products or become AI-native.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">2. Amazon and Meta struggle to hire and keep engineers</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Amazon and Meta seem to be kicking themselves after laying off or pushing people out of their jobs.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">Amazon makes higher offers to its own former engineers</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I was surprised to read this news, reported </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bb126c53-d5a6-4a91-95d0-15ad9cae5ed8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">by Business Insider</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Amazon wants former employees back, including some it laid off.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The company is reaching out to eligible former employees about open roles across Amazon, including in its cloud-computing and AI businesses, according to recruiter emails obtained by Business Insider and a company spokesperson.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In one outreach last month, Amazon’s AI agent organization, led by AWS VP Swami Sivasubramanian, invited former employees in AI and machine learning fields to discuss new roles through what a recruiter called “Swami’s Boomerang Reengagement Initiative.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This move is unexpected because Amazon’s hiring and firing policy – well known for over a decade – has been explicitly to </span><em>not</em><span> rehire people who used to work at the online retail giant! Instead, Amazon always opted for entirely new hires.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the deepdive “Inside Amazon’s engineering culture,” we covered the main incentive Amazon has to fire people: its own annual, 6% unregretted attrition (URA) target:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Each organization has an URA target which is usually at or above the LE (Least Effective) performance review target. Because of this target, managers have very little incentive to coach people on their team in the LE bucket. In what seems like perverse incentives, managers who would help one of their direct reports improve and get out of the LE bucket might have to find someone else on their team to put on Focus and then PIPs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">URA has become similar to a sales target for SDMs in recent years at Amazon. L7+ SDMs who would not meet their URA targets could expect this failure to be reflected in their ratings. A lower rating could affect their total compensation target.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One easy way to hit this URA target is to log a departing employee’s “regretted” attrition as “unregretted” instead, which helps fill the 6% quota – at the expense of that person who wouldn’t be eligible to come back to Amazon.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>But now, Amazon is dangling “internal level offers” to folks who might boomerang, I have confirmed with insiders there. </strong><span>A software development manager (SDM) told me that a tactic to woo people back is an “internal level offer.” This is the type of compensation that tenured engineers in the role usually earn, and different from what Amazon offers new joiners whose pay is at the bottom of the salary bands.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Basically, “boomerangers” are being offered more money than new, external hires, and are being rehired at their old level. Amazon is throwing money at getting people to return. The question is whether this will be enough to tempt them back after their previous experience there.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>This boomerang program suggests that Amazon is having trouble with recruitment. </strong><span>I wonder if the company has even reached out to “URAs” because they know managers game the URA systems in order to hit quotas. Amazon’s struggles suggest it has run out of experienced engineers with sufficient AI experience. This would mirror our finding in the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c099deb9-bca1-4854-8625-a5d07e63f9ca?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">2026 job market deepdive</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Catch-22:” nobody finds each other. Hiring managers struggle to find experienced folks, who barely get any replies when applying for jobs. How’s that work?”</p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">Meta does need engineers, after all</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Meanwhile, at Meta, several teams that were downsized need more engineers, and they’re asking for more headcount at the VP level. This comes only five months after the company laid off 10% of engineers and re-allocated 20-30% of them to AI training tasks, One engineer on one of these teams posted a succinct analysis of what’s happening:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">🤡</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meta’s case seems to be a head scratcher: the company encouraged engineers to use AI, and most devs became “AI-native,” but then Meta decided to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dc8e4327-ecb4-40a5-921e-42d8e4243127?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">lay a bunch of them off</a><span> and push out even more with forced reassignments. The tech giant then panicked two months ago after experienced, long-tenured engineers </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ed8ea4b9-9ce2-46ee-8810-297f577e7d1a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">announced</a><span> they had quit for better working conditions and more appreciation at places like Anthropic, OpenAI, or startups. Meta’s $1M+ retainer offers were </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ed8ea4b9-9ce2-46ee-8810-297f577e7d1a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">not enough</a><span> to stop the resignation wave.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Surely someone could have predicted that building out new systems like Meta’s Muse AI assistant would need more engineers? Especially as the new AI systems introduce new challenges in load, security, reliability, etc.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>VPs of Engineering at Meta are now doing “listening tours.” </strong><span>In April, the social media platform made it very clear that engineers are a commodity who can – and will! – be laid off whenever the company decides, or be reallocated to work they never signed up for and don’t want to do. A few months later and engineering leadership does now care about engineers, who have been given a forum to air their grievances to VPs – whose decisions were likely the cause of said gripes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I also hear the quality of food and snacks has suddenly improved.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meta clearly wants to retain engineers, especially after a Reuters article </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1143d42b-1481-4691-a8d3-b6265e7e01f4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">revealed</a><span> in January that the company wanted 60% fewer engineers, and to coordinate the largest-ever layoffs in the history of the company. Last I checked with engineers at the company, last week, OpenAI and Anthropic are still having pretty much unlimited free pick in poaching anyone and everyone they’d like to, without coming across any resistance from the engineers they reach out to. Why would they?</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">Meta also needs more managers</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meta kicked off the trend of reducing the number of middle managers in 2023, but it now needs more managers in its AI division, Business Insider </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/73f1ec53-000d-4dd3-8afa-854b6f653bfa?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reports</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Meta wants some of its employees to be managers again.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The social media giant has been asking some individual contributors in its Applied AI (AAI) division to transition back into management roles as part of a recent reshuffle, four people with knowledge of the matter told Business Insider. This program is opt-in, a person familiar said.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is the same division from which Meta reassigned 20-30% of engineers, so it would make sense that they would need more managers now. Still, Meta itself feels extremely reactive in how it operates, but it does pay top-of-market, which can motivate staff to put up with more chaos than they would elsewhere. But every move like this reinforces </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c3133100-f56f-416c-b5a0-229c11c9b229?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">a mercenary culture</a><span> where money is the sole reason people stay.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">3. Opus 5.5 released and it’s good</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Another new model from Anthropic, this one called Opus 5.5. The feedback has been universally positive, as I’ve gathered from engineers:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Superb coding</strong><span>: for coding, it feels as capable (or perhaps even more!) than Fable 5.1</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Cheaper</strong><span>: it </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d7c8eb59-81b3-45ca-920d-0562f8337c46?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">costs</a><span> 60% less to use than Fable 5.1 – which is a big difference! ($4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens, vs $10/$50 for Fable 5.1)</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Anthropic published Code reviews to vanish sooner rather than later?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Marc Brooker is a Distinguished Engineer at AWS, works on AWS S3, and is known for having high standards in software engineering. He has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/54642213-d536-4312-ac7b-58a55625738d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">written this</a><span> about the future of code reviews (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“There’s been a ton of talk about the role of humans in code review, and when and how humans should be signing off on changes.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>I believe that, long-term, humans have no role in routinely reviewing code.</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Short-term, many teams do it for good reasons. Quality. Understanding. Compliance. Those reasons exist, but we should be (and are) working on ways to make them go away.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The “mixed mode” where humans look at some code reviews, assisted by review tools, is also valuable today. But probably even more transient.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The idea that humans will reliably look through code to find the increasingly rare issues that automated tools miss seems like a fantasy.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>What does the future [without code reviews] look like?</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Review tools, powered by LLMaaJ-style techniques, static analysis, and automated reasoning methods. Principled approaches to testing and validation (PBT, DST, model-guided fuzzing, etc). Correct-by-construction techniques.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The combination of these things will lead to (and in many cases already lead to) better outcomes than traditional code review, both for large and small issues. Soon, much better outcomes than code review.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The days of Code review as a tool for increasing software quality appeared numbered, and the end may already be here (but unevenly distributed).</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>But what about code review’s value as a learning tool?</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That’s a harder one, and the solution is going to come as part of a much larger industry-scale raising of the level of abstraction developers work at from “in the code” to “in the specification” (or “in the requirements” or “in the feedback”).</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Some level of understanding of and mechanical sympathy for the implementation layers will still be a valuable skill. But day-to-day interaction and understanding will be entirely at a layer above.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>I see this transition as inevitable. </strong><span>In some places, it has already happened. In others, it still sounds entirely unbelievable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But it’s going to happen.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Marc’s takes are eye-catching after we discussed </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2c76e213-033b-4bbf-b97b-62ae5666abe2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">what’s happening with code reviews</a><span> two weeks ago. Since that deepdive, I’ve already seen many more signs in several startups – and even in Big Tech – that code reviews are effectively </span><em>already</em><span> dead. Instead, engineers glance through the AI code and approve with no comments. At most places, it’s just not possible to keep up with 5-10x as many reviews as there were a year ago.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>I appreciate Marc’s careful analysis. I can see highly regulated companies hold onto human – or “mixed” – code review for much longer. I also expect a surge of interest in verification methods outside of testing, be it in approaches like fuzz testing, lightweight formal methods, or even “proper” formal methods. </span><em><span>We previously covered </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f63fa684-ad87-4eed-91c9-f0a4276e0e10?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">formal methods and AI with formal methods expert Hillel Wayne.</a></em></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxNzI0NTg4OSwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3OTAyNjg1NzIsImV4cCI6MjEwNTg0NDU3MiwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.idara3tL36EtPfeTnzsUt5YbaaoAFGV1DWKjxq5bM5I?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>A web application can appear quite simple from the outside. A user submits a form, the application saves the information within the form, and a screen displays it later when the user wants to see the information. When the information is no longer needed, the information can be deleted from the system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, inside a growing system, the same information or data point can exist in several places. For example, a database holds the original record. A cache might store a copy of that original record for faster access. A search engine index can store some fields of that record to make search more intuitive. An analytics pipeline might produce reports from it. Lastly, backups may preserve earlier versions of that record.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each of these copies has its own purpose, update schedule, and overall lifetime within the system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The lifecycle of data shows how information can enter a system, become useful, spread to other components, become old or stale, and eventually be deleted. Thinking about this lifecycle helps connect decisions that might otherwise seem separate, such as database design, performance, reporting, storage costs, recovery, and privacy.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we are going to look at the entire data lifecycle from creation to deletion and the decisions that need to be taken at each step.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 to and changing with AI. We explore why Maggie starts projects with pens and notebooks, what distinguishes design engineers from other designers, and why understanding engineering constraints leads to better collaboration with engineers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We also discuss how Maggie uses jigs to gain more control over AI agents, why human judgment and style still matter when models can generate designs, and how inconsistent AI capabilities can mislead us.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong>Takeaways from the conversation with Maggie</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/403bcefe-b2f3-4218-b42b-952ddb4a4483?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/KZSzF0KEFRg" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Post-graduation, one potential career path led to a job inventing torture techniques for the US army. </span></strong><span>Maggie said ‘no thanks’ and resolved to work in tech instead. Maggie studied cultural anthropology and her background has helped her through her tech career to date. Software is built by people and relationships matter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Maggie got a frontend engineering education from illustrating React tutorials. </span></strong><span>She spent four years as an illustrator at the developer education company </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/93fef6cf-936d-4262-8dc0-8ceb09e34aa5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Egghead</span></a><span>, rising to art director. To illustrate the lessons, it was necessary to understand what she was drawing: React components, useEffect, and JavaScript functions. </span><em><span>Note from Gergely: I followed Maggie’s work after her excellent illustrations work on Dan Abramov’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/347d69c9-94c3-4c6a-9390-75dabf33d4d0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Just JavaScript course</span></a><span>. Here’s an animated explainer by her for that course:</span></em></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="394" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/8af1d675-3d71-4a19-8aae-b829cc5bef37?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/1548e56b-dc1e-4c77-90b0-54c88ebd020e_394x270.jpeg","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":270,"width":394,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="394" height="270" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dn7v!,w_394,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1548e56b-dc1e-4c77-90b0-54c88ebd020e_394x270.jpeg" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. Some folks believe the best UI interface already exists.</span></strong><span> In 2021, the AI startup where Maggie worked was trying to launch a new interface to speed up scientific research using LLMs – a year before ChatGPT was released. Months of intense work went into a “new UI for AI”, but it turned out that scientific researchers didn’t want innovations like infinite canvases with cards, composable Notion-like documents, and more. They wanted the same, simple tables they were deeply familiar and comfortable with! Maggie says the experience taught her that starting with a familiar primitive is sensible – even when innovating.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>4. The nomenclature matters! Also, problem solving is at the heart of design – just like in engineering.</span></strong><span> Maggie sees design and software engineering as related by being about problem solving. The difference lies in the materials. Coming up with the names and verbs to describe new things which will then be adopted and used by people can be hard work. Easy when building an online sneakers store, harder when building a new product for AWS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>5. Notebooks are an important part of the designer’s toolkit. </span></strong><span>Maggie often starts her projects by sketching out ideas. She finds it faster to sketch out an idea by hand than to describe it to a tool like Claude Code. Plus, when you sketch out an idea physically, it will still be there in the notebook the next day. In contrast, if it gets put into a tool instead, it’s a lot harder to go back to it, dozens of prompts later!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>6. Maggie regularly builds her personal Figma called “Jigs,” </span></strong><span>which is also the name of a woodworking device that helps with a specific job. She regularly asks a coding agent to build a prototype that has sliders and color pickers so she can tweak it in realtime, like having a personal Figma!</span></p><div Maggie has stopped looking at the code at work. </span></strong><span>When a PR is generated, she doesn’t look at the code, and this approach fits when building prototypes. Once she knows what to build, she composes a detailed spec, listing out how the agent will verify its work. Previously, she did keep an eye on the code, but that’s not needed with the new generation of models.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>8. Planning with AI agents breaks when there’s too much text. </span></strong><span>“I have this theory that planning is a really bad experience at the moment,” Maggie says. “An agent grills you with a set of choice A, B, or C questions a hundred times over. By question 20, you’re quite tired and your brain starts shutting down [because] you can’t make this many decisions in this short of time. Also, it told you A is recommended. Then you just start being like, ‘Yep, enter A, I agree with you.’”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>9. “Capability gaslighting” is when frontier models convince users they’re an expert but fail the same task the next day. </span></strong><span>Maggie coined the term “capability gaslighting” for how models impress users before failing badly soon afterward. Too often, we keep believing in models because we’re convinced they’re capable. The same is true for agents, so we should be vigilant when working with LLMs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>10. We need new types of artifacts for humans and agents to work better together, Maggie believes</span></strong><span>: “There’s this world that agents live in: there’s weights and models and skills and MCPs,” she says. “Then you have your human side: it is physicality and texture and light and materials and all these things agents don’t understand. Trying to find artifacts that allow us to meet in the middle and create stuff together is a really hard challenge because you’ve got two totally different types. I just find myself frustrated that agents cannot look over my shoulder, looking at my notebook and understanding what I’m drawing, and how they cannot help me move my ideas along.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>11. Engineers should try treating the AI agent as a patient tutor when learning about design: </span></strong><span>As engineers, we can ask AI agents to teach us about design: they’re good at explaining things like when to change up line height, what a good sidebar looks like, or how many characters to squeeze into a line, etc. In the past, acquiring product design skills was hard, but AI agents make it a bit easier</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>I hope you enjoyed this episode, and many thanks to Maggie for educating all of us engineers!</span></em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe They can write code, summarize documents, and answer questions across many subjects. However, an application may still need something the model does not provide consistently. Its answers might omit important details, the way it classifies information might confuse similar categories, or its responses might ignore a particular expected writing style.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These things don’t mean that the model is not intelligent or doesn’t have knowledge. Often, it has the underlying capability but needs additional help applying it according to specific expectations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That is the purpose of customizing a model. One way is to follow clearer instructions and provide better information. But when those also leave gaps between the expectation and reality of the model, further training needs to be imparted. Techniques such as LoRA and QLoRA make that training more practical by reducing the resources needed to adapt an existing model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we are going to look at the various strategies to customize and fine-tune a model.</span></p><div learning points in brief:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>When instructions and information are not enough</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How fine-tuning changes a model</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>LoRA: Learning a smaller set of changes</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>QLoRA: Reducing the memory footprint of the model</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Tuning the techniques into a training process</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>When Instructions and Information Are Not Enough</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The natural starting point in customizing a model is prompting.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A prompt describes the task, identifies constraints, and specifies what a good answer should contain. For example, we can add examples of the type of answer we expect to give the model a clearer demonstration of the expected behavior. This approach is called few-shot prompting.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This simple approach can be quite effective. The task of summarizing a document becomes more useful when it specifies which details matter and how the summary should be organized. Many applications need no customization beyond well-designed instructions and prompts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, instructions can’t provide information that is missing. If an answer depends on an internal document or a recently updated policy, the application must provide that material explicitly to the model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the main technique for addressing this requirement. It finds relevant information in an external source and includes it in the model’s input. The model can then use that material when producing its answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Prompting and RAG both work through the information supplied during a request. They can guide behavior in a big way, but they don’t ordinarily change the model’s learned parameters.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Sometimes, recurring weaknesses remain. A model might still struggle with specialized document categories or keep producing summaries that highlight the wrong details. While adding more examples as part of every request may help, it also increases the amount of input the application must maintain and process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is where fine-tuning offers a different option. In fine-tuning, we can train the model on many examples so that the desired behavior becomes more firmly learned as part of the model’s default behavior.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is not an absolute division between behavior and knowledge. Fine-tuning can also teach facts. However, retrieval remains useful when information changes frequently, or answers must be traceable to an external source.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Fine-Tuning Changes an Existing Model</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As you might be aware, a model’s behavior depends on billions of numerical values called parameters or weights. Many of these are weights that influence how information moves through the model’s calculations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>During pretraining, these values are adjusted using large amounts of training data. A text-generating model learns to predict the next token, which is basically a piece of text such as a word, part of a word, or punctuation. This process helps develop broad language capabilities within the model. Models intended for conversation usually receive additional training to follow instructions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, fine-tuning continues from an existing model using a more focused dataset. Since fine-tuning builds on top of capabilities that are already present within the model, it reduces the amount of training required for specialization.</span></p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A common approach is supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In SFT, each training example contains an input and the response the model should produce. Examples might pair documents with approved summaries, messages with category labels, or programming requests with suitable code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>During training, the model predicts the desired response tokens. The training process measures how well those predictions match the supplied targets. This measurement is called the loss. Backpropagation identifies how the trainable parameters influence that loss, and an optimizer adjusts them to improve the predictions going forward.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, a model may initially answer a classification request with a long explanation. However, training examples that repeatedly pair such requests with short category labels encourage the model to aim for more direct responses. The same principle applies to the details provided in summaries or the conventions followed while generating code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Across many examples, these adjustments can increase the likelihood of desired behavior based on new inputs. Since the saved changes persist, future requests don’t need to include the entire training dataset in every input they provide.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Supervised fine-tuning does improve things, but it has limitations. Writing explicit examples for every possible scenario the model might encounter is impractical. This is where reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) provides further refinement. The process begins with the model generating multiple responses to various prompts. Human raters then rank these responses based on quality, helpfulness, and safety. These rankings train a separate reward model that learns to predict scores human raters would assign to any response.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0"
