auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>SFT and RLHF describe how examples teach the model. On the other hand, LoRA and QLoRA describe how that training is carried out efficiently. The same instruction-response dataset can be used with these different approaches.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The more straightforward type of fine-tuning, known as full fine-tuning, allows every model parameter or weight to change. This provides flexibility, but is also quite expensive. Training must store the weights along with the information used to calculate and apply their updates. Also, intermediate results that were produced while processing examples must also be stored.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is why a model that fits on a GPU for generating answers might require much more memory for full fine-tuning. Longer examples and larger groups of examples processed together only push the resource requirements higher.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, as we discussed, the model already has a pretty good grasp on the language aspects. Adapting it to a particular task may not require adjusting every parameter independently. This possibility leads to LoRA.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>LoRA: Learning a Smaller Set of Changes</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LoRA stands for Low-Rank Adaptation. It is a form of parameter-efficient fine-tuning, which means it reduces the number of parameters that training needs to update.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LoRA keeps the original model weights frozen. They still perform their calculations, but training doesn’t modify them. Instead, small trainable components are attached to selected calculations inside the model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These additions are called adapters. They learn adjustments that are combined with the original calculations. This way, the overall output generated by the model changes because the model now uses both its existing capabilities and the learned adjustments.</span></p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An adapter operates inside the model. It doesn’t wait for a completed answer and rewrite it afterward. Its adjustments influence the internal processing that eventually produces the answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These small components are implemented using two compact tables of numbers, called matrices:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The first creates a compact intermediate representation from the input for a calculation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The second turns that representation into an adjustment that can be added to the original result.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Training changes the values in these small tables.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The compact representation belongs only to the adapter. The original model still performs its full calculation, so the adapter doesn’t have to recreate all the capabilities the model already possesses. The reason this works is that changes often have shared patterns. If we want a model to write concise technical explanations, we don’t need it to relearn grammar, programming, and sentence construction. Much of that ability already exists within the original base model. Training simply needs to adjust how those abilities are applied.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The term “low rank” refers to representing such an adjustment through a limited set of coordinated patterns. These are learned numerical relationships, rather than explicit rules provided by a developer. Therefore, LoRA restricts how the model can change. This restriction saves resources, but it also creates a trade-off. A small adapter may be sufficient for one task and too limited for another.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A setting called rank controls the adapter’s capacity. Higher rank gives it more room to learn varied adjustments, while increasing its size and training overhead. Values such as 8, 16, 32, and 64 are possible starting points. But a higher rank is not automatically better.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the beginning of standard LoRA training, the adapters contribute no change. Therefore, the combined model starts with its original behavior. Their adjustments develop as training processes the new examples. LoRA can also target selected attention calculations, which help the model relate different parts of its input, as well as other transformations inside its layers. Targeting more locations provides additional opportunities to adapt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The savings are related to managing updates for a much smaller collection of parameters. The original model is still necessary and performs substantial computation. LoRA makes training more manageable without turning the underlying model into a tiny model.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>QLoRA: Reducing the Memory the Frozen Model Still Needs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LoRA solves much of the expense of updating parameters, but the frozen base model still occupies memory. For a sufficiently large model, storing those weights can remain a major obstacle.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>QLoRA, or quantized LoRA, addresses this by combining LoRA with quantization.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Quantization stores numbers using fewer bits and a more limited set of possible values. It preserves an approximation of each original weight while discarding some numerical detail. This reduces storage, but it can also introduce errors into the model’s calculations. The overall model structure and parameter count remain the same. Each weight simply has a more compact representation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>QLoRA commonly stores the frozen base weights in 4-bit form. The adapters remain at higher precision, allowing training to make even finer adjustments to their values. Depending on the implementation, adapter parameters and calculations can use 16-bit or 32-bit formats.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/6cedf28f-d911-4e9d-a77f-4bf1f3a22320?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We need to distinguish between storage and computation here. A weight can be stored compactly and reconstructed as a higher-precision value when needed for a calculation. This reconstruction creates an approximation, but doesn’t recover the complete detail discarded during quantization. QLoRA uses this approach to perform the base model’s calculations, combines their results with the adapter adjustments, and trains the adapters using the combined output. The original quantized weights remain frozen.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Although training updates only the adapters, the original calculations still influence what those updates should be. Even if we freeze a part of the model, it is not removed from the learning process. Only the weights are not changed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since the adapters learn alongside the quantized model, they adapt to that actual combination. They can help recover task performance affected by compression, although they cannot be assumed to correct every quantization error.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For a fixed memory budget, this can make it possible to customize a larger model than ordinary LoRA would allow. The original QLoRA work has shown great savings, but the practical requirement still depends on the model, length, batch size, and training implementation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Compressed weights are only part of training memory. The system still needs adapters, their update information, intermediate results, and working space. Lower memory use also does not guarantee proportionally faster training.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LoRA and QLoRA are therefore closely related. LoRA reduces how much must be trained, while QLoRA also reduces the space occupied by the frozen base model.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Turning the Techniques Into a Training Process</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first decision is to choose a suitable starting model. The model should already perform reasonably well in the required language and task. This is because a model that struggles with basic instructions or lacks the necessary capabilities will not do wonders even after customization.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before training, we need to establish a baseline using a carefully developed prompt. This provides a clear picture of the remaining problems and a reference for measuring improvement.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Next, we need to prepare examples that demonstrate the desired behavior. For extraction, include messages with different wording, missing information, and details. For summarization, provide varied documents and consistent examples of how it should be structured.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Correctness is important here because training rewards agreement with the supplied answers. If similar inputs receive contradictory labels, the model can receive conflicting guidance. If approved summaries contain unsupported claims, those claims also become part of the behavior being taught.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Next, we need to prepare separate training, validation, and test sets:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Training examples cause parameter updates.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Validation examples help compare settings and choose a saved version of the model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Test examples provide a final assessment after those decisions.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Duplicate or closely related examples should not leak across these groups.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The training configuration then controls capacity, update size, and resource use. For example:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Rank and adapter placement determine how much adjustment LoRA can learn. This learning rate controls the size of training updates. Excessively large updates can destabilize learning, while very small ones can produce little progress.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Batch size describes how many examples are processed together. Larger batches generally require more memory. Gradient accumulation allows several smaller batches to contribute to an update. This helps a lot when memory is limited.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Another memory-saving option is gradient checkpointing. It keeps fewer intermediate calculation results and recreates some of them when needed. This trades additional computation for lower memory use and can complement LoRA or QLoRA.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Training duration is measured in epochs, where one epoch means one pass through the training dataset. One to three epochs can be an initial experiment, but repeated exposure isn’t always better. Training longer can make the model overly dependent on the examples it has already seen. This problem is called overfitting. A warning sign for this is when performance on training examples improves alongside worsening performance on validation examples. The useful checkpoint may come before the final training step.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The evaluation process should measure the actual task. For example, classification needs correct labels, extraction needs correct values, and summarization needs faithful coverage of important details. Well-formed output alone doesn’t establish correctness.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, we need to check the capabilities the application still depends on. An adapter can improve one behavior while weakening another, even though the original weights remain frozen. The combined model’s behavior has changed, so it must be evaluated as a whole.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Using the Specialization in an Application</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LoRA training produces adapter weights that can be saved separately from the base model. These files are generally much smaller than a complete model, but they require the compatible base checkpoint to function.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Keeping adapters separate makes it easier to manage different specializations. Where the serving software supports it, the same base model can be used with different adapters for different tasks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another option is to merge the adapter’s learned adjustments into the base weights. This produces a standalone customized model and removes the need for separate adapter calculations. The resulting file contains the full model, so it loses the storage advantage of an adapter-only file.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Merging and quantization support depend on the implementation. We need to evaluate the exact version that will be deployed, since changing its numerical representation can affect results.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The application can still use prompts to specify the current task, RAG to supply relevant information, and validation code to check outputs. Fine-tuning improves learned behavior while these other features continue handling their own responsibilities as before.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Fine-tuning is useful when a model has broad capabilities but needs more reliable specialization. It learns from demonstrations and reflects recurring response patterns more firmly in the model’s behavior.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LoRA makes this less expensive by learning compact adjustments while preserving the original weights. QLoRA reduces the memory requirement further by storing those frozen weights at lower precision.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Neither technique replaces good examples or careful evaluation. The goal is a measurable improvement on new inputs, at a cost the application can support. A clear task, a suitable starting model, and representative training data matter as much as the choice of training method.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: Emoji', 'Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: 400;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em><span>Before we start, a special announcement to paid subscribers: if you’re in San Francisco on Thursday, 5 November, join me on the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/38ce79e0-285d-4fa1-baf7-576ca504ca96?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">System Update with The Pragmatic Engineer event</a><span>. This is an evening with OpenAI, Linear and DoorDash and myself, organized by Sentry. We get into what AI-augmented automations they’re running in prod, and how it’s going, in an off-the record and raw conversation. Seats are limited, but as a paid subscriber, I’m aiming to prioritize your RSVP: please you use the code TODO</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI is changing how us software engineers build software, and developers’ tool preferences are rapidly evolving with it – like how AI coding harnesses have gotten very popular. Likewise, future versions of the world’s leading operating systems look certain to feature more support for agentic tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To find out how things are changing, we talked with the folks at tech giant Microsoft who shared in detail their plan for Windows, and how AI will play a part. It comes after the company’s previous AI efforts led to it being dubbed “Microslop” by some users online.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Windows team’s vision is opinionated and includes building new agentic primitives, alongside reversing some decisions that have annoyed engineers. Microsoft wants developers who have shunned the system to return. The big question is: will it succeed?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For more, check out a previous article on how </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fa762701-df41-4c7f-bb51-025eae16539a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the leading Linux distribution, Ubuntu, is changing, thanks to AI</span></a><span>, with a focus on hardware support for GPUs, NPUs and DPUs, a bet on local-first LLMs, and a focus on AI developer tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, we cover:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>How many devs use Windows anyway? </span></strong><span>It’s hard to get exact numbers, but macOS appears far more popular at startups than Windows, while Linux may also be on track to overtake Microsoft’s OS in developer popularity.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Agent identity & discovery.</span></strong><span> Windows ships with native support for agent identification, plus a centralized registry of locally available MCP servers to be included with the OS.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Isolate agentic tools.</span></strong><span> Microsoft is building an OS-agnostic isolation mechanism that should make it easy for developers to build agents that run tools safely.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Running models locally</span></strong><span>: Windows is betting big on local models. WindowsML is a new hardware abstraction layer for building and running local AI models across GPU, NPU, and CPU. The OS aims to ship Small Language Models (SLMs) without requiring an NPU in the future. We’ve also seen an impressive demo of a local model running on a Surface laptop using NVIDIA chips.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Building agents on Windows:</span></strong><span> one goal of the OS is to allow building of agents with opinionated frameworks and libraries that devs can just assume are available.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>More dev-friendly</span></strong><span>: Windows was plagued by questionable product decisions that resulted in a cluttered Start menu and search, to the chagrin of many developers who lost interest in the OS. Microsoft wants them back and is addressing criticisms – </span><em><span>finally!</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Linux on Windows (WSL): </span></strong><span>Windows ships with an embedded Linux called Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). It’s proving quite popular with devs. Windows embracing Linux might just be the strategy to get devs to switch from both native Linux and macOS, as counter-intuitive as this strategy sounds.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Windows & hardware:</span></strong><span> since its early days, Windows has gone out of its way to support a wide variety of hardware. The OS was x86-based from the beginning, but Windows on ARM is starting to finally look like a good alternative. A look into why ARM support took so long, and the upcoming NVIDIA collaboration.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’ve Consider how a rogue agentic application can impersonate a user and not self-register as an agent – which in a sense is how viruses operate by using legitimate OS functionality for illegitimate purposes. That’s why Defender, Microsoft’s antivirus software, is becoming “agent aware” and scanning Windows for known local agent activity like it scans for viruses.</p><div underline;"><span>ODR</span></a><span>) is the centralized place where agents register and discover available MCP tools. ODR manages and runs MCP servers locally, and also comes with connectors for core operating system components like the File Explorer or System Settings.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s say you want to build a specialized Photo Organizer Agent; the organizer agent organizes photos in the user’s Photos folders by theme and starts by running an image classifier to understand photos’ themes, then puts them in the relevant folder, such as ‘</span><em><span>parties</span></em><span>’, ‘</span><em><span>outdoors</span></em><span>’, ‘</span><em><span>baby photos</span></em><span>’, etc.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As such, the Photo Organizer Agent needs the ability to read and change the user’s local files, which starts with Windows ODR finding an MCP connector for the file access capability. After discovering File Explorer, the agent uses File Explorer MCP to access and modify files in the user’s Photo directory.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: However, the process ID that ODR sends back to the agent is ODR itself: the Photo Organizer Agent talks to the File Explorer MCP through ODR!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By putting itself between the MCP client and server, ODR can inspect payloads going back and forth. This is a useful choke point because it enables Windows to detect potentially dangerous behavior. However, this proxying behaviour is as yet unconfirmed by Microsoft, so it remains to be seen how they use it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>3. Isolate agentic tools</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Tools are external programs that an agent uses to perform actions on the operating system, such as native OS tools, third-party app calls, or even programs written by an agent. Granting agents rights to execute tools potentially means code execution, so it’s essential the agent tools run in isolation to ensure the user’s files and session aren’t reachable by agentic tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Microsoft Execution Containers</span></strong><span> (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aef28adb-0819-406e-9e24-0aec5ff80526?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>MXC</span></a><span>) is a new, in-development agent containment technology by Windows. Developers can use MXC to spawn agentic tools in isolated environments called sandboxes, and agent access within the sandbox environment is configured through MXC </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/02a904fa-9ced-4046-a278-14d9b478a820?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>containment policies</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Containment policies are JSON-based config files that describe network, filesystem, UI, and execution restrictions. The image below illustrates how MXC works:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 different containment tech & OSes</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s say you’re building an agentic application like OpenClaw. This application will necessarily have to use tools to do its job and can use file operations, web operations, shell commands, and more. These are potentially dangerous operations, as OpenClaw executes them through MXC’s spawnSandboxFromConfig() method, which spawns a new contained process in which said tools can run safely. The process containment technology used depends on the containment policy config. MXC doesn’t do the containment itself and uses multiple existing containment technologies for that; for example, on a Mac, it would use </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f8888044-39f9-4d8e-b3a6-00624c94b39b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>seatbelt</span></a><span>, a process containment layer built into the Mac OS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Speed versus safety tradeoff: </span></strong><span>some containment mechanisms are faster to start and cheaper to run than others. For example, starting a new process is faster than starting a new Windows session or a new virtual machine. At the same time, running a new process in the existing user’s Windows session potentially exposes the user’s filesystem to the new process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MXC allows developers to adapt the containment level to the sensitivity of the operation being run. Multiple containment levels are available in Windows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Process containment</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Session containment</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Running WSL containers</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Lightweight Hyper-V containers</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Full virtual machines</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Choosing the right level of containment is a trade-off between the blast radius and speed of execution. chores, and how MXC provides finegrained control over agent isolation. MXC is under development, but already runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Developers therefore get a unified way of containing external tools across operating systems.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>4. Running models locally</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e132cbc6-d8f0-41e5-b847-5a7712c250f8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Windows ML</span></a></strong><span> is a hardware-agnostic layer for running AI models locally on Windows. Its goal is to do for AI what DirectX did for computer graphics: abstract away hardware complexity, regardless of the underlying model’s architecture.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Windows ML is Microsoft’s second attempt at building a hardware-agnostic layer for running ML models. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0f6c2145-b586-4925-8bed-f94132c565b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>DirectML</span></a><span>, the first attempt, is a library for running machine learning tasks on GPUs built on top of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5a22ab27-4ff2-4a8f-b3b8-b11afb09ada1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>DirectX 12</span></a><span>, Microsoft’s graphics library used for running games on Windows, released in 2019.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, an obvious question is how is Windows ML different? They say that Windows ML offers two improvements over DirectML:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>#1: Higher level abstraction & better hardware coverage</span></strong><span>. DirectML is a low-level library where developers have to manually build the inference pipelines from simple mathematical operations, worry about memory layout, etc. Being based on DirectX, DirectML only worked with GPUs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, Windows ML is based on the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8c653bbd-199d-4690-8d4a-47440d36afb5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Open Neural Network Exchange format</span></a><span> (ONNX), an open format for representing and running neural networks. Neural networks built with all popular machine learning frameworks can be converted into the ONNX format called ONNX graph and run on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/eabf5226-275d-45c9-900f-59fc4261fedf?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>ONNX runtime</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>ONNX runtime is an open source, cross-platform system for training and running neural nets defined in the ONNX format. Windows ML provides developers a framework that runs on a broader range of silicon, including GPUs, NPUs, and CPUs from all major vendors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>#2: No driver-update bottleneck:</span></strong><span> Windows ML wraps the ONNX runtime and abstracts away the hardware-specific runtime optimizations by providing hardware-agnostic APIs. Each hardware vendor implements this API for its own hardware through the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9e899d05-155d-49f7-9979-7b998c18acc3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Execution providers</span></a><span> (EPs) concept. With DirectML, new runtime optimizations had to be done via driver updates which took six months to get meaningful adoption.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Windows ML loads EPs when they are needed, depending on the user’s hardware. For example, if a user has an NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPU, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7a375fca-fa6f-4dc1-8224-54fe25446e08?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the NVIDIA Tensor RTX execution provider</span></a><span> is downloaded and used to maximize GPU performance. Hardware vendors build and submit PEs to Microsoft for certification and testing before they can be used with Windows ML. Most execution providers </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dfcb20c7-ce5f-4ac0-a8bf-a74a8a55026f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>available today</span></a><span> are also available on GitHub.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: href="https://substack.com/redirect/0cd12683-5112-4aba-830e-8bf3c4231ad2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Small language models</span></a></strong><span> (SLMs) are embedded within the operating system. Without them, developers would have to ship models with their apps, or call cloud-based models. Even if running local models should be easier with Windows ML, it’s still not worth the effort if you want to add simple functionalities to an app.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>For example, running a sentiment analysis on some text in an application used to involve calling a hosted AI model in the cloud. On top of incurring app running costs, it can also add lag to the app, whereas with embedded models developers can assume the models are already there, and use them as any other local library. </span><br><br><span>For example, </span></span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b40816a9-cb00-495b-b43e-37c33f166dfb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the Aion-1.0-Instruct model</span></a><span> is built into Edge, Microsoft’s web browser. Accessed through the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6f3314d3-8b53-4b74-ad0e-cb983d8c4c28?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Prompt API</span></a><span>, Aion model allows developers to build apps like sentiment analysis with a few lines of code. Here’s an example from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b098c9dc-78ec-48f9-82e6-e8a28944be2d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Microsoft’s website</span></a><span>:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px underline;"><span>Source</span></a><span>)</span></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even a simple web application can now have LLM-powered features like sentiment analysis without having to continuously pay for tokens. The demo is JavaScript-only, but versions for native apps and other languages are also expected to be available when it’s released.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Teams being able to run their own models is becoming increasingly important, especially in the corporate sector, driven by escalating costs, mode availability questions such </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/443fde75-4527-46f5-935f-839f54a8c3be?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>as those recently raised with Fable</span></a><span>, and compliance issues.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Running models locally also unlocks a hybrid approach, which is well aligned with a trend among tech companies we </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/362cd763-34b9-488c-a6ee-4dca0b487c44?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>recently covered</span></a><span>, where tech companies have successfully shifted their LLM workloads to cheaper models for simpler requests, and only use frontier models for advanced reasoning. By running models locally, some agentic jobs could be executed with local LLMs, and more complex jobs delegated to a cloud-hosted frontier model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Running local models on a next-gen Surface laptop with NVIDIA GPUs is impressive. </span></strong><span>At Microsoft, Scott Hanselman showed us a pre-release Surface laptop with NVIDIA GPUs running Qwen as a local model, hooked up to GitHub Copilot. This local model churned out tokens at a rate of ~40 tokens per second! Once such laptops become widely available, coding-related use cases could become a lot more viable, running locally.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>5. Building agents on Windows</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Besides Windows being agent-friendly, Microsoft is also investing in the agent building toolchain to simplify agentic app development by providing a rich agent building framework.</span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f45d3b79-6ca8-4a5e-9afd-28256feca533?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Microsoft Agent Framework</span></a></strong><span> (MAF) is a C#, Python, and Go library designed to make it easy to build agents on Windows. More than just a wrapper around LLM APIs, the framework supports agentic primitives like tools, multi-turn conversations, persisted memory, and even a workflow engine. It’s the main option for .NET developers and integrates well with agentic primitives in Windows mentioned earlier. The following snippet illustrates how easy it is to use MAF primitives:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure You don’t have to stitch together old message exchanges to keep the agent’s context up to date; the built-in session capability handles it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MAF natively supports all the above-mentioned agentic primitives that the OS ships with. Developers can use it to build native agentic apps for Windows which in turn comes with useful agentic primitives built into the OS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Windows being an opinionated runtime environment for agents has a few advantages for developers who build agents:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Simpler to build Windows-native agents.</span></strong><span> Developers can assume certain agentic capabilities in the OS. For example, local MCP capabilities can be discovered and registered via ODR, and there’s a simple way to contain tool execution.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Support to run local LLM models.</span></strong><span> Windows ML will make it easy for developers to include custom local AI models within their apps. Previously, developers had to consider hardware variants and bundle different SDKs with their app. Windows ML should abstract all of that away.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Company-level agent administration.</span></strong><span> Larger companies can have control over agents in their enterprise. Whitelists dictate which agents can run, limit what access they have, and have observability of agents in the network.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>6. More dev-friendly</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As alluded to by the existence of terms like ‘Microslop’, Windows isn’t such a popular operating system among software developers these days. This is a change from when the OS couldn’t be avoided during its </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/62fd7e3d-9fe9-43e8-886f-28b2d68320d2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>XP</span></a><span> era, when Windows enjoyed a 90+% market share. But that changed as apps transitioned to web and mobile, driven by two forces:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Switching operating systems easier than ever</span></strong><span>. Most modern apps are web based and run on any OS. Before, when considering a switch to a new OS, you had to check if your favorite desktop apps worked. This is no longer an issue as modern desktop apps are on the web, or use cross-platform frameworks like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fe742241-c5f2-41cf-a6d8-322bb71f128f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Electron</span></a><span>.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Windows got less developer-friendly. </span></strong><span>Windows became less configurable over time, with stricter requirements on what users could do – exactly the things developers dislike. Also, command line support lagged behind Unix-based operating systems, and Microsoft kept ignoring developers’ configurability complaints.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Basically, developers were frustrated with Windows as they felt it wasn’t prioritizing their use cases. For example, OS configurability, flexibility, and system details that developers value were largely ignored:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Mandatory Microsoft accounts: </span></strong><span>these became compulsory with Windows 11. Windows is the only OS to mandate a vendor-specific account to use an OS. With macOS, an Apple account is only needed to use Apple services; the OS can be used without one.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Clutter and ads: </span></strong><span>The start menu and Windows search grew cluttered with irrelevant content like app suggestions, web search results, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7edbd9a2-9cd5-4e6f-93b4-a8a7131aa312?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>even ads</span></a><span>, with no way to change things.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Lack of customization:</span></strong><span> With Windows 11, customization of the taskbar’s size, position, auto-hide, and similar tweaks, were no longer possible</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since then, the Windows team seems to have gotten the memo that devs dislike all the above changes, and Windows chief Pavan Davuluri </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4862ca6c-3638-40f0-b15f-375f271ac06d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>committed</span></a><span> to making Windows better for developers. Now, there’s now less clutter in the start and search menus, and Windows simplified its most used menus. Non-critical features are now optional:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Start menu size can be changed and no longer has to occupy the whole screen, which is critical on smaller laptops.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Various tips and app recommendations can now be removed from the Start menu</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Here’s an example of how broken Windows Search was, until recently. </span></strong><span>Below, a user searches for a text file (“New Text Document”) that contains the word “motorola”. Before, on the left-hand side, Windows Search returned too many irrelevant web results and suggestions. But after a recent change, it now returns only the relevant document.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure fire-and-forget operation. The script will make the necessary changes to the OS and even handle multiple reboots for settings that need it. The overall operation can last an hour or more, but the whole process is hands-off for the user.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Microsoft Account still required:</span></strong><span> Frustratingly for some users, a fresh Windows installation </span><em><span>still</span></em><span> requires a Microsoft account. While </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e10dcf87-19ea-45e1-9004-16f96c826e25?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>multiple</span></a><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/de06a652-9755-4b2a-9b6f-a0ad31b4f499?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>bypasses</span></a><span> exist, we fail to see how such a strict requirement can make Windows attractive to devs when no other OS mandates a vendor-specific account just to install it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Being forced to log into an account like this is annoying, but the privacy controversy over the ‘Recall’ feature dealt a major blow to Microsoft’s already-damaged reputation with devs: </span></strong><span>In May 2024, Microsoft </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/45207783-e6b0-4436-b299-ed3baf882f54?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>announced</span></a><span> Recall, a Windows feature that allows users to search their previous activity. Recall took screenshots of the desktop every few seconds, indexed them, and made them searchable. It was marketed as a photographic memory for a computer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There were two major problems with this:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No ability to turn it off:</span></strong><span> Microsoft </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/22b8e125-6f4f-4d60-8fd1-e5b96e1685a5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>wanted</span></a><span> to make the feature non-removable, using resources on all machines, whether or not a dev wanted to use the privacy-invading feature.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Comical security approach</span></strong><span>: Recall shipped with a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3c480b6f-56f7-420c-b561-f58b47451d18?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>serious security flaw</span></a><span>. Screenshots did not remove sensitive information like banking data or other personal data, and all the information was kept in a local SQLite database in plaintext! That meant any local app or rogue user could read the data without the user’s consent or knowledge.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s unclear why Microsoft thought it would be acceptable to ship a poorly implemented, privacy-invading feature without an opt out. Microsoft later </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ac93ff8c-7c10-46c9-b898-5ab036f4a8e2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>cancelled</span></a><span> the June 2024 general launch of Recall, and the final version was released to the public in April 2025, as an opt-in, non-mandatory, feature. But much damage was already done. Why would devs trust an OS vendor that shipped core OS features so carelessly, and only changed course after large – and predictable! – public uproar?</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>7. Linux on Windows (WSL)</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Historically, developer tools were </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5d7f975b-df1e-4947-ad42-cb83740efac7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Microsoft’s strong suit</span></a><span>; after all, its very first product was a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2ac896b4-08c2-400f-807a-423bf9465567?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>BASIC interpreter</span></a><span>. Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, Visual Studio was the gold-standard IDE for building desktop applications: fast and snappy at a time when competing IDEs like Eclipse or NetBeans were painfully slow. Until around 2010, the Visual Studio debugger was the industry standard for debugging tooling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But Microsoft’s development tools became less popular as the tech industry focus moved from desktop apps to web apps, and later to mobile apps. The issue was that Microsoft’s tools were Windows-only, while web and mobile apps were built using open source technologies. So, developers increasingly chose Mac or Linux. In response, Microsoft is making Windows more Unix friendly to try and win developers back.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) has addressed the issue by shipping Windows with an embedded Linux since 2016. With WSL, Linux is accessible in Windows by typing wsl in the command prompt. Previously, running Windows and Linux on the same machine required </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6a064d46-018d-4bfc-bb73-95df2bc5a334?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>dual-booting</span></a><span>, and during that process the user had to pick which operating system to use. Switching back to the other OS required a reboot, and sharing data between the two operating systems was cumbersome. Linux could read or write Windows disks, but not vice versa.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>WSL doesn’t just run Linux inside Windows. It has also allowed running native Windows apps from WSL for a few years now. For example, let’s say you have the following a web server access log file:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure
