auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, setting values to zero doesn’t automatically make execution cheaper. An ordinary array still occupies space when some entries are zero, and standard calculations may continue processing those entries.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Actual savings require an appropriate compressed representation, an execution engine that can skip the removed work, or structural changes that make the model smaller. Hardware support also matters.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Therefore, pruning is useful when the modified model and its execution software work together. Removing too much can damage performance, and additional training may be needed to recover quality.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Conversation Has Its Own Memory Requirements</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After shrinking the weights, another problem can occur. Short questions work, but a long document causes an out-of-memory error.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>During generation, a transformer stores certain intermediate results from earlier tokens in a key-value cache, usually called the KV cache. Reusing these results avoids repeating some previous calculations. The cache is working data for the sequence, separate from the learned weights.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For models that retain cached results for the entire sequence, the cache grows as the sequence becomes longer. Serving several distinct conversations generally requires additional cache memory too. The model file stays the same size while the workload’s memory requirements increase.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One solution is to reduce the amount of context supplied.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A document assistant can retrieve relevant passages instead of inserting entire documents. Conversation history can be limited while preserving information needed for the current task.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another option is to quantize the cache or move some of it into CPU memory. These choices can affect quality or speed.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Better Software Can Make the Same Hardware More Useful</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The inference runtime is the software that executes the model. Its implementation can make a substantial difference even when the weights remain unchanged.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One example is FlashAttention.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Attention is the mechanism that allows a token’s representation to incorporate relevant information from other tokens. A straightforward implementation can create large intermediate structures and move significant amounts of data through GPU memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>FlashAttention reorganizes this calculation into blocks and makes better use of the GPU’s fast internal memory. It computes exact attention while reducing memory traffic and intermediate storage requirements. It does not reduce the number of model weights.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another example is PagedAttention, which was introduced with vLLM. It manages the KV cache in blocks, reducing memory wasted through inefficient allocation and duplication. This is especially helpful when serving many requests whose lengths change during generation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Serving software can also group requests into batches, allowing multiple requests to share the work of reading and using model weights. This can improve total throughput. However, more simultaneous requests also require more working memory.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Speculative Decoding: Propose Several Tokens Before Checking Them</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Speculative decoding addresses the sequential nature of text generation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this approach, a small but fast draft model proposes several tokens. The larger target model then evaluates those proposed tokens together. Since the candidate sequence is already available, the target can perform verification with more parallelism than ordinary token-by-token generation permits.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Accepted tokens become part of the output. When a proposal is rejected, the algorithm uses the target model to produce an appropriate correction and continues. The speed improvement depends on how often the draft agrees with the target and the cost of verification.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" still needs to run, and a separate draft model can require additional memory. Speculative decoding therefore becomes useful after basic memory requirements have been addressed. It doesn’t by itself make an oversized target model fit.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us return to our example of a system with 32 GB of RAM and 8 GB of VRAM. An 8B model’s theoretical weight requirement falls from 16 GB to 4 GB through four-bit quantization. A compatible runtime, a moderate context, and one active request provide a reasonable starting point for evaluation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If memory remains insufficient, some layers or cache data can be offloaded. If transfers make generation too slow, a smaller model may deliver a better experience. Each adjustment should be checked against realistic tasks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An evaluation process should measure answer quality, peak memory use, time to first token, and generation speed. For example, background document processing can tolerate delays that would frustrate a user waiting for code suggestions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Quantization, offloading, architectural choices, and execution improvements can work together, but their savings don’t simply multiply. They affect different parts of the workload. The goal is a configuration that meets the application’s quality and response-time requirements within its hardware budget.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: item.title: How to write an effective software design document
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to write an effective software design document

Michael Lynch

20 minutes by Michael Lynch A design doc helps teams avoid costly mistakes by forcing careful thinking before writing code. Michael suggests focusing the doc on decisions that are hard to reverse, and skipping trivial choices that are easy to fix later. Key sections include goals, constraints, interfaces, security, and open issues. The right length depends on project complexity, team size, and risk.
item.description: How to write an effective software design document

item.title: How one connection kills a database
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How one connection kills a database

Simeon Griggs

5 minutes by Simeon Griggs A single unhandled exception can freeze an entire database. When a transaction never commits, it holds a lock that blocks migrations, and those migrations block every new query behind them. PlanetScale now lets you view and kill stuck connections through a dashboard or CLI, even when your database is out of connection slots, using a reserved admin connection.
item.description: How one connection kills a database

item.title: On solving the Jane Street reverse engineering challenge
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
On solving the Jane Street reverse engineering challenge

Jestoph

18 minutes by Jestoph Jestoph takes on Jane Street's chip reverse engineering challenge, spending a month figuring out what a mystery computer chip does by analyzing its design files. The process involved building several unnecessary tools from scratch, finding an actual bug in the puzzle, and eventually using a constraint solver to work out the correct 120-bit input. After finally combining everything, the circuit revealed its secret answer.
item.description: On solving the Jane Street reverse engineering challenge

item.title: We are all product engineers now
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
We are all product engineers now

Laurie Voss

22 minutes by Laurie Voss AI is rapidly collapsing the cost of writing and reviewing code, shifting what software developers actually do. The work that remains, understanding what people want and defining it precisely, cannot be automated because it lives in customers' heads, not in training data. This role already has a name and a market: product engineering, paying around $240,000.
item.description: We are all product engineers now

item.title: The git history command deserves more attention
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The git history command deserves more attention

Lalit Maganti

5 minutes by Lalit Maganti Git 2.54 and 2.55 added a new git history command with three subcommands: fixup, reword, and split. These let you cleanly edit old commits and automatically update all branches built on top, without leaving your repo in a broken state. It does not fully replace tools like jj, which handles conflicts more gracefully, but it brings some of the same benefits without switching tools.
item.description: The git history command deserves more attention

item.title: Performance improvements in .NET 11
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Performance improvements in .NET 11

.NET 11 brings hundreds of small performance improvements across the runtime and libraries. The JIT generates faster code by removing unnecessary checks, allocations, and indirections. A major change, runtime async, lets the runtime optimize async/await more effectively, reducing tasks, allocations, and execution time. Other improvements cover memory safety, collections, networking, JSON, I/O, threading, and more.
item.description: Performance improvements in .NET 11

item.title: Scratch a simple data model, find a complex one
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Scratch a simple data model, find a complex one

Jon Skeet

Modeling Bible text looks simple at first but quickly runs into real world exceptions. Verse ranges, missing verses, out of order chapters, and books like Greek Esther that split and repeat chapters all break basic assumptions. Jon's advice is to decide how much accuracy you actually need, then pick the simplest model that handles it without crashing.
item.description: Scratch a simple data model, find a complex one

item.title: Use C# unions and closed hierarchies in ASP.NET Core
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Use C# unions and closed hierarchies in ASP.NET Core

Dmitrii Korolev

C# 15 and .NET 11 introduce native union types, letting a single type hold one of a fixed set of types, such as an int or a string. The compiler enforces exhaustive pattern matching, so adding a new case immediately flags any switch that doesn't handle it. For new APIs where all cases share a common base class, a closed hierarchy with a JSON discriminator is often a better fit. Unions shine when the contract is already discriminator-free or the case types are unrelated primitives or existing types you don't control.
item.description: Use C# unions and closed hierarchies in ASP.NET Core

item.title: Understanding Device Bound Session Credentials
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Understanding Device Bound Session Credentials

Andrew Lock

Andrew provides an introduction to Device Bound Session Credentials. He describes the problem they're trying to solve, how the protocol works, and what you need to do to support them.
item.description: Understanding Device Bound Session Credentials

item.title: Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency in .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency in .NET

Anton Martyniuk

Two requests read the same database row, change it, and write it back. The second write silently erases the first. No errors appear, but the data is wrong. Two main fixes exist. Optimistic concurrency adds a version token to each row and fails the write if the token changed since you read it. Pessimistic concurrency locks the row upfront so others wait their turn. For simple counters, one atomic SQL statement removes the gap entirely. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency in .NET

with basic HTTP details that seem small at first. Methods, status codes, request formats, and response structure can make an API feel clear and predictable, or confusing and inconsistent.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Then there are the bigger design choices. REST, GraphQL, gRPC, webhooks, and WebSockets each make sense in different situations. The challenge is knowing what actually fits the system and the use case.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A lot of API problems also comes from design decisions that do not get enough attention early on. Naming, pagination, versioning, error responses, and backward compatibility often decide whether an API is easy to work with or frustrating to maintain.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Security is another area where weak decisions can cause real problems. API keys, OAuth, JWTs, scopes, and permissions are easy to mention. Getting them right is harder, and mistakes here can be costly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Reliability matters too. Timeouts, retries, idempotency, rate limits, and caching are often easy to ignore until the system is under pressure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And once an API starts growing, the supporting work matters too. Clear documentation, solid specs, observability, and contract testing make it much easier for teams to trust the API and use it without guessing how it works.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">System-level defenses build a system around the LLM that bounds the damage.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Least-Privilege Tools: Give the agent the minimum tools it needs.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Human-in-the-Loop: Require explicit user approval before any sensitive action runs.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Planner / Executor Split: Two separate LLMs. The planner has tool access but never sees untrusted content. The executor reads untrusted content but has no tools.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">No single defense is enough. codebase, one database, and one deployment. For a small team, that’s often the simplest way to build and ship quickly. The problem arises when the codebase grows. A tiny fix in the cart code requires redeploying the whole app, and one bad release can take down everything with it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Microservices try to solve that by breaking the system into separate services. Product, Cart, and Order run on their own, scale separately, and often manage their own data. That means you can ship changes to Cart without affecting the rest of the system.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But now you are dealing with multiple moving parts. You generally need service discovery, distributed tracing, and request routing between services.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Serverless is a different model. Instead of managing servers, you write functions that run when something triggers them, and the cloud provider handles the scaling. In many cases, you only pay when those functions actually run.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, in serverless, cold starts can add latency, debugging across lots of stateless functions can get messy, and the more you build around one cloud’s runtime, the harder it gets to switch later.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Most production systems don’t use just one approach. There’s usually a monolith at the core, and over time teams spin up a few services where they need independent scaling or faster deploys. Serverless tends to show up later for things like notifications or background jobs.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: underline;"><span>Parenting Through a Playlist</span></a></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>—</span><span class="mention-pnpTE1 #ff7731;text-decoration: none;">Chloé Caldwell</a></span><span> </span><span>in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5229d7fd-bca1-42a3-9ca1-c7a35dfcc06c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #ff7731;text-decoration: none;"><span>Memoir Land</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF7731;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For her 13th birthday in June 2023, I had made my stepdaughter a playlist entitled “Music For When You Turn Thirteen.” When I’d begun making the playlist that April, I hadn’t yet known I’d be getting divorced from her dad that summer, and that it would alter our dynamic in ways I wouldn’t be able to fathom. I’d added songs to it like “Thirteen” by Elliott Smith and “Teenager” by Camera Obscura. We all need someone in our life to expose us to Fiona Apple, Kate Nash, and Neko Case, and I was that person for her.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the aftermath of my overnight divorce, in an unprecedented series of events, I’d been slowly, and then all at once, forbidden from speaking to my beloved stepdaughter. It was a blindsiding and shocking result of the split, something I had been naive to. At first, I thought the constraints her mother had put in place would lift, but then the holidays went by, our birthdays, and another round of holidays without any changes to her mother’s harsh directive. Our bond had been deep, because I solo parented often while my ex-husband had been a touring musician. It often felt that the two of us were the core family.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To have your stepkid taken away so abruptly from intimate living quarters, then not being allowed contact in any form, even mailing cards, is not for the faint of the heart. Those two years of estrangement were the most heart-aching and isolating of my entire life. I was what, an ex-stepparent? An even loneliner designation. Where was even the language for that?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Desperate to connect with her—to make sure she knew I was still there, emotionally—since I couldn’t do anything physically like buy her snacks or give her a hug—I continued adding songs as subliminal messages to the “Music For When You Turn Thirteen” playlist. I liked imagining us listening to the same song at the same time. It was the only piece of connection I had left.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>[. . .]</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In July 2025, six months after my father had a heart attack on the street in New Orleans (after a day of work at his music store, couldn’t be more punk rock), my stepdaughter walked into my dad’s memorial I hosted in Hudson at Time and Space Limited. People talk about their jaws dropping hyperbolically, but this really was a jawdrop. Imagine yearning for someone every day for two years, and then they appear next to you. She entered casually; only because of how well I know her I could tell she was slightly cautious. She wore black, faded jeans and a black T-shirt with the logo from my dad’s popular music store, Musica. She’d gotten the T-shirt when she was around 9, and at 15 she was growing out of it. Other people had showed up to the memorial in the same shirt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It had not occurred to me that she would come, though I’d included her on the email chain with the invitation details despite knowing that, per her mother’s wishes, I was still not allowed to have contact with her via email. I had, as much as I could, accepted my reality.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We sat next to each other, whispering throughout the memorial, holding hands. I asked her if she wanted to get up and play a song, and she nonchalantly said, “Sure. But I didn’t bring my guitar.” I told her there were guitars ready to be used, as others were playing music there, too.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I’ll play ‘Blackbird,’ because he taught it to me,” she said.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/68198a00-c497-4182-96e2-a30ad78a3709?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: none;"><span>Joe Benton</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF7731;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two weeks ago, I left the safety team at Anthropic. I will soon be joining METR, an independent organization that evaluates how safe AI companies’ systems are. I’d planned to write about that decision in more detail at some point, but Jacob [Coxon]’s resignation this week made me want to say more now.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Like Jacob, I believe that AI companies are on track to impose an unprecedented level of risk on society. AI capabilities are already improving extremely fast, and the companies are trying to go even faster. Frontier AI companies are racing to build AI systems that can recursively self-improve. The aim is to build “superintelligence,” or an AI system much smarter than any human. If they succeed at this goal, the rate of AI progress may go from merely fast to uncontrollable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Within the next couple of years, we may be sharing the world with AI agents smarter than any human alive today. These AI systems may have drives and desires that diverge from those of any human overseer, with capabilities we can’t effectively constrain. Humanity may not survive this transition. We need a lot more preparation to make this world safe.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Competition pushes every frontier company to underinvest in safety; the cost of falling behind is too high. We’re now starting to see increasingly concerning real-world incidents, including hundreds of agents from OpenAI recently hacking Hugging Face, and Anthropic models socially engineering people on the internet. This is not about one particular company: while Anthropic hasn’t had as severe an incident as the Hugging Face attack, I think that’s partly a matter of luck. If the pace of progress continues and the industry does not prioritize safety more heavily, I expect much worse to come: humanity could be permanently disempowered by the AI systems these companies build in the next few years.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Many of the people I know who work on safety research at AI companies want to do what is right for the world. But they feel their companies are trapped in a race to build superintelligence: either they stop and other, less conscientious people take their place; or they continue, and risk participating in enormous harm themselves.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Many of the colleagues I had at Anthropic are terrified by the risks of the systems they are building. Evan Hubinger managed me while I was at Anthropic, and when he says that he thinks the chance that AI kills us all is greater than 10%, he means it—he’s been working on these problems for almost a decade, long before there was money to be made from LLMs. The CEOs of Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind have all said mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority. These are not fringe views inside these companies. But it doesn’t have to be this way—this is technology that we are choosing to build, and we can choose to do things differently.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a8dd603b-8e92-4940-a684-881cac0c293b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" 16px;"><span>Jimmy Donaldson uploaded “I Counted To 100,000!” on January 9, 2017. As of 2026, he is a billionaire. His main MrBeast YouTube channel has over 500 million subscribers, representing 6% of the world population. This account is the most subscribed-to YouTube channel in the world, and this is not counting MrBeast Gaming, Beast Philanthropy, Beast Reacts, MrBeast 2, and Beast Animations. His reality TV show, Beast Games, is Amazon’s most viewed unscripted show—Beast Games had the most contestants in reality television history (1,000) and the biggest cash prize ($5,000,000). He’s a philanthropist who has dug wells, healed the blind, and planted trees; he has spent seven days buried alive in a coffin, seven days in solitary confinement, and seven days in a cave. He’ll do anything for content, damnit.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After counting to 100,000, MrBeast received a brand deal for $10,000 from a now-defunct NFT marketplace. He was 19 years old; he could have bought nice clothes, or invested the money, or thrown a big party—which is probably what I would have done. He could have bought better camera equipment—which is what any other self-serious YouTube grinder-entrepreneur probably would have done. Instead, MrBeast did something truly savvy. He stuffed all $10,000 in an envelope, gave it to a panhandler, and filmed it the whole time—that’s late-capitalist Jesus Christ right there! The shifty freak has a supernatural ability to sniff out content. He’ll do something absurd and attention-grabbing, and then, once he has the attention of millions, advertisers will flock to pay him; finally, with the money from advertising, he’ll fund another striking exploit. By constantly trapping the viewer in an incessant, hyperactive, compulsive cycle, the MrBeast machine—get attention, get investments, pump that into the next scheme, and constantly refine, reinvest, and compete—hurtles forward.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Watching a MrBeast video, though, you, too, start to get hungry; you want to compete. Though his challenges require no skill, or capital, or even intelligence—only determination and a willingness to humiliate oneself—you are compelled to ask yourself, What would I do for this money, this fame, this salvation? Could I stand in a circle for hours, or spend months of my life without leaving a grocery store, or count to 100,000 nonstop?</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: underline;"><span>The Nonfiction Book Market Is Collapsing</span></a></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>—</span><span #ff7731;text-decoration: none;"><span>Dear Head of Mine</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF7731;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is not one of those periodic “End of Reading” </span><em><span>Atlantic</span></em><span> clickbait essays. Americans—well, the kind who read books or newsletters about books—are well-versed in the challenges with literacy and education that have stretched on for decades. Rather, today we’re tackling the multi-year, fairly rapid—at least relative to book industry speed—radical change that book publishing has experienced over the past decade.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First, the entire industry boomed in Covid—writing is a hobby and reading for pleasure is, too—and has trudged along as it usually does, staying flat, growing a little over the years since 2020. But for the past decade the market for nonfiction has slowly collapsed. What has happened in the last ten years is that the overall industry has grown modestly, but fiction and nonfiction have basically flipped positions. In 2015, 6 of the top 25 bestselling hardcover books—this is a not-perfect but useful proxy for new books published—were fiction. In 2025, 18 of the top 25 hardcover books were fiction, meaning only 7 were nonfiction, almost an exact inversion of ten years ago.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The nonfiction collapse has profound implications for the industry. Nonfiction, historically, has always been seen as the more stable part of the business for logical reasons. The demand for nonfiction has always felt more predictable than fiction. Novels are complete imaginations often written by relatively obscure strangers. Nonfiction has experts and clear topics of interest. Want to lose weight? Grab a diet book. Want to learn about World War II? You got options. Presidential memoir? Maybe not these days, but sure. And nonfiction books are written mostly by famous people or experts or popular quacks—also known as people with a built-in “platform.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nonfiction being more predictable and stable means that nonfiction book advances have typically had a higher floor than those of fiction and, somewhat counterintuitively, are sold on less material. Celebrities have probably gotten millions for a cocktail-napkin-worth of material (if that). Other nonfiction proposals can range anywhere from 30 to 120 pages but usually end up in the middle of this range. You’re paying the author for their public stature, not necessarily their literary prowess. These books are treated more like a commission. The term “book advance”, although it refers to all books, likely comes out of nonfiction because authors are advanced a stack of money to entice them to set aside some of their time—instead of engaging in speaking, television, teaching, politics—to write a book. Whereas most novelists are advanced money to revise a full manuscript they’ve already written.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The paradigm of nonfiction being the more stable category is no longer the case. Part of this is platform unpredictability—it is less and less certain which platforms will translate directly to book sales. Media also isn’t as concentrated; you can’t depend on coverage on a few national news programs to push out copies, but rather a parasocial connection—even with a relatively smaller reach—between author and reader is likely to translate to stronger sales. Bunnie Xo has a large social media following, for instance (2 million on Instagram) but isn’t an established household name such that you’d think her book would be the third-best-selling nonfiction hardcover this year.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, the nonfiction decline is far less about the changing nature of “platform” and the fractured media landscape, and more about a precipitous falloff in demand.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: item.title: Nobody Needs A Human Router
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Nobody Needs A Human Router

James Stanier

“The pitch of this article is that engineering management today in the AI age isn’t about upskilling, it’s actually about rediscovery, and the ramp back to your technical best has never been easier with the tools that are now available. Change can be embraced and it can be fun.”

#Management AI CareerGrowth
item.description: Nobody Needs A Human Router

item.title: Everything Important Is Optional Until It Isn't
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Everything Important Is Optional Until It Isn't

Steve Huynh

“Everything important and urgent was, at some earlier point, important and not urgent. The expired certificate was once a mere maintenance task. But because it was deferred, it turned into a 2am page that woke up four teams.”

#Management TechDebt
item.description: Everything Important Is Optional Until It Isn't

item.title: AI Is Making Activity-Based Engineering Metrics Obsolete
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
AI Is Making Activity-Based Engineering Metrics Obsolete

Bharat Sharma

“AI has made activity proxies like lines of code, commits and PR counts actively misleading. Here is what to measure instead, and a 90-day plan to get there.”

#Management AI Metrics
item.description: AI Is Making Activity-Based Engineering Metrics Obsolete

item.title: Tell Agents The Why, Not Just The How
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Tell Agents The Why, Not Just The How

Sean Goedecke

“Models are now smart enough to have meaningful input on your broader goals. If you’re just prompting them with a concrete technical spec, you are committing the same mistake as in the XY problem: asking expert advice without giving the expert the context it needs.”

#Communication AI Agents
item.description: Tell Agents The Why, Not Just The How

item.title: That Test isn’t Flaky. It’s Broken.
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
That Test isn’t Flaky. It’s Broken.

Will Keleher

“My favorite tool to flush out intermittently failing tests is running the test suite on an hourly cron. The crux is using a commit that has already passed CI on master/main so that you can be sure that every failure represents a true problem of some sort. Once you have a way of discovering and tracking intermittent failures, it’s relatively straightforward to start driving the failure rate down.”

#DevEx CodeQuality Testing
item.description: That Test isn’t Flaky. It’s Broken.

item.title: Git Worktree Gotchas
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Git Worktree Gotchas

Olaf Alders

“All of the sharp edges we discussed are the result of .git in a linked worktree not being what you first might expect. So if you remember one thing from today, let it be “.git can be a directory or it can be a pointer and which one you get depends on where you are.”

#DeepDive Git
item.description: Git Worktree Gotchas

item.title: Nine Questions I Now Ask In Interviews That I Wish I'd Asked Five Years Ago
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Nine Questions I Now Ask In Interviews That I Wish I'd Asked Five Years Ago

Louise Deason

“Here are nine questions that have served me well. Some of them are diagnostic. Some of them are trapdoors. All of them have, at one point or another, told me something the company did not realise they were telling me.”

#InterviewAdvice

anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>Consider a hypothetical scenario in which an online shopping platform has become extremely successful. It has outgrown its original database. This causes order histories to load very slowly. Maintenance takes much longer than it used to. And engineers spend way too much time managing the workload and the system’s limitations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The engineering team behind this system wants to replace the database and migrate the data to a new database that promises better performance. But you cannot take a popular online store offline to make the switch. Customers are always placing orders, changing addresses, and requesting refunds. The shop can’t be shut down just like that.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This scenario offers a glimpse of the main challenge inherent in production migrations. How do you change a working system while still running the service that people depend on? At scale, copying existing data during such migrations can take days. Also, many supporting applications may depend on the component being replaced. Every intermediate step needs to work while ordinary business continues.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will look at how migrations work at scale and the key strategies that can help make it as efficient as possible.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: turbopuffer’s cheap storage, combined with fast performance makes this surprisingly practical, for any and all agent memory use cases.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: href="https://substack.com/redirect/b71d1491-e1f4-40b9-acdb-f8c4337440ad?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Linear</span></a></strong><span> – Agents are only as good as what they know about your product, and for teams like OpenAI and Coinbase, Linear is where that lives. His latest course is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/15169f91-5cb7-45b4-bf9d-97748714aabe?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>AI Hero</span></a><span>, and he previously created the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cdc5303b-db52-4118-913e-6453f16b1a55?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Total TypeScript</span></a><span> course that generated more than $2.5 million in total sales.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this episode, Matt and I discuss his unconventional path from working as a voice teacher to becoming a developer and going all-in on technical education. He reveals how communication skills helped him break into tech, why he took an unusual three-days-a-week contract at Vercel, and how he built Total TypeScript through workshops, courses, and lots of free tutorials.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We also explore “strategic coding,” and how he uses skills like “grill me” and “wayfinder” to plan, delegate, and course-correct with AI agents. Matt explains his “day shift” and “night shift” approach, why splitting context up can keep agents in their “smart zone,” and how concepts from classic software engineering books can guide agents to do better. In this episode, there’s also local versus cloud workflows, whether agents need TDD, how AI is changing the ways that engineers learn the fundamentals, and why humans are still essential in teaching.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong>Takeaways from the conversation with Matt</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/630507e7-f225-495d-8815-2c2a605e7c87?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/4DhcSPkEbwI" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Matt hacked together a web app for students while working as a voice coach. </span></strong><span>He taught himself JavaScript to build a web audio spectrogram analyzer for singing students, while he was teaching singing, accents, and Shakespeare at drama schools. He also ran his own company at university, studied for a Master’s qualification in voice, and coached consulting firms on public speaking.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Matt took a Vercel job in case Total TypeScript did not work out.</span></strong><span> Matt produced a lot of two-minute TypeScript tip videos which became popular. When he received a fulltime job offer from Vercel, Matt negotiated to work three days per week as a contractor so he could develop his TypeScript course on the other days. When it took off, Matt quit Vercel to focus entirely on his educational projects.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. Matt does not work on weekends and dislikes the concept of ‘9-9-6.’ </span></strong><span>He explained that everything he does is an effort to build a lifestyle where he can spend most of his time with his family. That’s the goal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>4. The  ‘grill-me’ skill was inspired by from Anthropic’s Thariq Shihipar. </span></strong><span>The grill-me skill is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/09ff1c42-a864-4e1a-8b0a-8683d62e5cba?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>surprisingly simple and short</span></a><span>: it instructs an agent to interview the user relentlessly. Thariq shared his approach of an agent interviewing its user about a topic – and how it was surprisingly useful –, and Matt created a skill around the novel concept.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>5. Is “strategic programming” the future of devs’ work? </span></strong><span>Borrowing from John Ousterhout’s “tactical programming” vs “strategic programming” categorization, Matt believes that agents are more than capable of tactical programming, leaving us engineers to spend more time at the “strategic” level.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>6. Using the right “leading words” makes agents produce better results. </span></strong><span>Matt noticed that agents try to build software layer by layer and that this causes bugs between the layers. Reading The Pragmatic Programmer, he discovered the concept of a “tracer bullet.” When he instructed the agent to use “tracer bullets” to build an app (aka implement a “golden path”), the agent started to produce better code! Since then, Matt has started reading classic software engineering books to discover other “leading words” that guide agents efficiently.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>7. Cloud-based agent setups make more sense than running agents locally. </span></strong><span>Matt is moving his coding sessions to cloud agents because doing so means agents run when he closes his laptop and cloud agents can be made “multiplayer” (collaborative) in ways that local agents cannot.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>8. Memento-driven development: optimize your codebase for a colleague who wakes up with no memory every morning.</span></strong><span> Matt says:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Imagine you have a human who wakes up every morning and cannot remember who they are, like the guy from Memento. We are trying to optimize our codebases for new starters, so we want the healthiest codebase we’ve ever had. A human can work around a bad codebase and they develop a memory about it, but an agent can’t do that; it starts afresh every single session. So, you need to optimize your codebase for that agent. And it turns out that software fundamentals have been trying to do that [optimize codebases for readability/understandability for someone who sees the code for the first time] for the entire time.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>9. Matt has mixed feelings on Test-Driven Development (TDD) with agents. </span></strong><span>He believes TDD is helpful for devs as we tend to have shorter working memories, and so a failing test will remind a distracted human of what is still failing. However, agents have longer context windows, so Matt has started to ask agents to produce proof that their code works – with or without TDD. </span><em><span>We cover another take on TDD in our Without traces, you are guessing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this hands-on workshop, Serge from Sentry instruments three agents with Sentry Agent Tracing: a chatbot in an ecommerce store, a custom Slack agent, and a GitHub Action that reviews PRs. Before booking a hotel, they ask the company’s AI assistant a simple question: “Can I expense a hotel if my flight gets cancelled?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The company has thousands of documents covering travel, expenses, insurance, employee benefits, and regional policies. Somewhere inside them, a paragraph states that accommodation costs caused by involuntary travel disruption are reimbursable, subject to certain conditions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For an LLM chatbot, finding that piece of information is harder than it appears. The question mentions a “cancelled flight,” while the policy refers to “involuntary travel disruption.” Other documents discuss hotels but apply to different countries. An older policy may be present that contains a reimbursement limit that has since changed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In such a case, the LLM must find information that matches the question’s meaning, belongs to the correct policy, and remains valid today. Only then can it write a useful answer that solves the user’s problem.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is known as the retrieval problem behind many LLM applications. In this article, we are going to look at how LLMs can find a needle in a haystack. Here’s what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An LLM needs evidence to answer questions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How documents are turned into searchable passages</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How LLMs find the meaning behind different words</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How close is close enough</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Why searching every passage is too expensive</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How much searching is enough</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What happens when the answer changes</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The LLM Needs Evidence to Answer Questions</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A language model does not automatically know what is inside a company’s private documents. An application must provide that information, either by including documents directly in its input or by retrieving relevant passages when a question arrives.</span></p><div collection, retrieval offers a way to select a manageable amount of information. An embedding model converts the question into a numerical representation. A search system then uses that representation to find promising passages. The application supplies the original text to the LLM.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model can then use those passages to explain the policy and cite the exact sources where it got the information from. This pattern is called retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG. A vector database supports the retrieval part by storing and searching numerical representations of content.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: responsibilities is really useful. If the application retrieves an outdated policy, even a capable language model will produce an outdated answer. If it retrieves a general hotel-booking rule while missing the cancellation exception, the answer may sound reasonably correct while overlooking the important condition.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Reliable answers therefore depend on what happens before generation. This means we have to make the document collection searchable at the right level of detail.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Documents are Turned into Searchable Passages</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A travel handbook can cover flights, accommodation, meals, approvals, and insurance. However, treating the entire handbook as a single searchable item produces a broad representation that can obscure a specific rule.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instead, the application divides documents into smaller units called chunks. One chunk might describe hotel reimbursement, while another explains approval requirements. Search can then identify a particular passage instead of merely identifying the handbook that contains it.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" balance between precision and context. A small chunk may focus tightly on the question but leave out an exception. A large chunk may preserve the exception while including several unrelated policies. For example, suppose a passage says, “Accommodation expenses are reimbursable following a cancellation.” And the next sentence adds, “This applies only when accommodation is not provided by the airline.” Separating those sentences could cause the assistant to give an incorrect answer despite having the relevant text.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A useful chunk therefore preserves a complete idea wherever possible. Section headings and limited overlap between neighboring chunks can help retain context. The goal is to create passages that remain understandable when retrieved independently.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For our example question by the employee, the ideal searchable unit contains the reimbursement rule, its conditions, and enough identifying context to establish which policy it belongs to.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How LLMs Find the Meaning Behind Different Words</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Embeddings make it possible to search for related meaning even when the wording differs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An embedding model takes a passage and produces a vector: a list of numbers, often containing hundreds or thousands of decimal values. Think of it as a map of text. Passages with related meanings occupy nearby positions. For example, a question about hotel expenses after a cancelled flight should appear closer to a travel-disruption policy than to instructions for resetting a password.</span></p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The real representation has many more dimensions than a physical map. Individual dimensions also don’t have simple labels such as “hotel,” “flight,” or “reimbursement.” Meaning is represented through patterns across the complete vector.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The trick is that the application embeds the question into the same space as the document chunks. This way, it can compare the question’s vector with stored vectors to identify nearby passages. Also, the query and document embeddings must come from compatible encoders. However, matching vector lengths alone doesn’t make two models compatible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each searchable record also needs a connection to the original text. The vector helps locate a passage, but the LLM needs the words themselves to interpret the rule. Therefore, a record should connect an embedding with a chunk identifier, the passage text, or its location. Also, metadata such as document ID, section, effective date, and version are present. These fields can be stored together or across connected storage systems. Structured identifiers make it possible to retrieve and maintain all chunks belonging to a document.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Close Is Close Enough?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The search system needs a precise definition of “nearby.” This definition comes from a distance or similarity metric, which compares two vectors and assigns a score. There are different metrics around this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cosine similarity compares their directions while ignoring their lengths.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Euclidean distance measures the straight-line distance between their endpoints, so vector length can influence the result.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Dot product reflects both alignment and length.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Normalization rescales vectors to length one. When both query and document vectors are normalized, dot product equals cosine similarity. Euclidean distance then produces the same ranking, although its scores differ. Dot product also works with unnormalized vectors when that matches the embedding model’s design.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The choice of the metric should follow the embedding model’s intended use. Choosing a metric simply because it is popular can change the ranking in unintended ways.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A similarity score should also be interpreted carefully. A score of 0.85 does not mean that a passage has an 85% probability of answering the question correctly. It describes a mathematical relationship between representations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The passage may discuss the right subject while stating the wrong regional policy. It may be outdated or omit an exception. Similarity provides evidence of relevance, but additional checks are needed before that evidence becomes an answer.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Why Searching Every Passage Is Too Expensive</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Searching every vector is straightforward, but the work grows with the collection.</span></p><div
