0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>What Does “memory” Mean for an LLM?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the context of LLMs, the word “memory” is used for several different things that should not be confused. Let’s look at each type in detail.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Trained Memory</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>During training, an LLM learns patterns from enormous amounts of data. These patterns are encoded in billions of numerical values called parameters or weights.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is why a model can explain JavaScript, recognize a common historical event, or write an email without receiving that knowledge in the current prompt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But this is not personal memory. If a user tells the model, “My preferred programming language is TypeScript,” a normal API response does not rewrite the model’s weights. The base model does not permanently learn that fact from the conversation.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Working Memory</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model’s temporary working memory is its context window. This contains everything the model can consider while generating its current response.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>What Happens During a Basic API Call?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider the simplest possible API request:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: <span class="line"><span>  “messages”: [</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    {</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “role”: “user”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “content”: “My name is Adam.”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    }</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  ]</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>}</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model might answer: “Nice to meet you, Adam.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Suppose the next request contains only this:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>{</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “messages”: [</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    {</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “role”: “user”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “content”: “What is my name?”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    }</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  ]</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>}</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model can’t reliably answer because the second request doesn’t include the name. The earlier request has already finished. And there is no private diary that exists inside the model that is kept updated.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For the conversation to work, the application must send the earlier exchange again:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>{</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “messages”: [</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    {</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “role”: “user”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “content”: “My name is Adam.”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    },</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    {</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “role”: “assistant”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “content”: “Nice to meet you, Adam.”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    },</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    {</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “role”: “user”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>      “content”: “What is my name?”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    }</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  ]</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>}</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now the model answers “Adam” because the name is visible in the current input.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most model providers have a stateless Messages API that requires the conversation history to be supplied for a multi-turn conversation.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Does Every API Call Really Start From Zero?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A new model invocation doesn’t typically start without any knowledge. The model still has several things:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Its trained weights</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Its general language abilities</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Knowledge acquired during training</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Safety and behavioral instructions supplied by the platform</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Everything included in the current context</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What it lacks is an automatically updated memory of this particular user or conversation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A better way to put it is that every response is generated from the model’s existing weights plus the context made available for that response. Information from the conversation history is not available unless the surrounding system carries it forward.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some APIs offer server-managed conversation state. In such a case, we don’t need to resend every message manually. We can provide a conversation identifier, and the server locates the previous messages based on that identifier to reconstruct the necessary context. This makes the API easier to use, but it doesn’t mean that the model has developed a personal memory.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How AI Chatbots Create the Illusion of Memory</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Suppose a conversation contains five user messages and five assistant responses.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When the user sends the next message, the application may construct an input that contains the following details:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>System instructions</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>User message 1</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Assistant response 1</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>User message 2</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Assistant response 2</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>User message 3</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Assistant response 3</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>User message 4</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Assistant response 4</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>User message 5</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Assistant response 5</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>New user message</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model receives all of this as one large input. For example, in the earlier conversation, the user may have mentioned a database problem, selected PostgreSQL, and asked for TypeScript examples. Therefore, it can continue the answers based on this path in a more natural manner.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To the user, this might feel like the model has remembered things from earlier. However, from the perspective of the model, those details are simply present in the text that is being processed right now. We can’t simply call it “fake memory” because there is real continuity at the application level. A better term for this is reconstructed memory or context-based memory.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Context Window is a Working-Memory Budget</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A context window of an LLM is measured in tokens. Tokens are small pieces of text. A short word may be one token, while a longer or unusual word may be split into several tokens.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The context window normally contains more than the visible conversation. It may also contain hidden instructions, tool definitions, search results, documents, and space for the answer. Imagine a hypothetical model with a 100K-token context window. An application might need to fit the following into that space:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>System instructions: 3,000 tokens</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Tool definitions: 8,000 tokens</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Conversation history: 55,000 tokens</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Retrieved documents: 20,000 tokens</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Current question: 1,000 tokens</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Remaining response budget: 13,000 tokens</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Once the available space is exhausted, the application can’t just keep adding information indefinitely. It must remove, compress, or replace something.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A large context window also doesn’t guarantee perfect recall. As the amount of information grows, it can become harder for the model to differentiate important facts from irrelevant, repetitive, or contradictory material. This degradation is also known as “context rot”. We need to select useful context even if we have a very large context window at our disposal. Therefore, the context window is both a capacity limit and an attention-management problem.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Why Long Conversations Become Expensive</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LLM APIs commonly charge for the number of input and output tokens processed. Let’s say each completed conversational round adds approximately 1000 tokens.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Request 1 processes approximately 1,000 tokens.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Request 2 processes approximately 2,000 tokens.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Request 3 processes approximately 3,000 tokens.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Request 10 processes approximately 10,000 tokens.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Across those ten requests, the application has processed approximately 55K tokens of input.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The visible conversation contains only about 10,000 tokens, but earlier parts have been processed repeatedly. A long system prompt, large tool definitions, and retrieved documents can increase this cost even further.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Longer contexts also increase latency. This is because more information needs to be processed before the model starts to answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Techniques like prompt caching can help alleviate costs, but they don’t create memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Providers can cache a repeated prefix such as the system prompt and previous conversation history. When the next request begins with the same content, the provider may reuse previously computed information. This can reduce cost and latency. However, cached tokens consume part of the context window. Caching merely changes how efficiently repeated context is processed. It doesn’t give the model unlimited memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Prompt caching is therefore an optimization, not a memory architecture.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>What Happens When the Context Window Fills Up?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is no single universal behavior that LLMs perform when the context window fills up. Depending on the API and application, several things may happen.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The API may reject the request because it is too large.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The application may remove the oldest messages.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A chat product may manage history using a rolling window.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The system may replace old material with a compact summary.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Some APIs also provide server-side compaction mechanisms.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Compaction is carrying forward important state in a smaller representation so that long-running interactions continue with lower context usage. This means a very long chat may not contain every original sentence in its active context. The model may instead receive something like:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Conversation summary:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The user is building an invoice service in TypeScript.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>PostgreSQL was selected as the database.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The API uses Express and Prisma.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The current problem concerns duplicate invoice creation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Previous attempts involving application-level checks failed under concurrency.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The summary preserves the central state while discarding greetings, repeated explanations, abandoned ideas, and low-value details. The tradeoff is that summarization is lossy. A small detail that seemed unimportant during summarization may become important later.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Main Techniques to Extend Memory</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Real applications usually combine several techniques to extend memory instead of relying on one. Let’s look at a few techniques in detail.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Sliding-window Memory</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A sliding window keeps only the most recent portion of the conversation. When new messages arrive, the oldest ones are removed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, the application might always retain:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The system instructions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The latest 20 conversational turns</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The current user message</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table simple, fast, and predictable. It works well when recent messages matter much more than older ones.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Its weakness is that once an old fact leaves the context window, it disappears. If the user mentioned an important requirement 30 turns earlier, the model may no longer be able to address it.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conversation Summarization</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Summarization periodically compresses older messages into a much shorter description. The summary stays in the context while the original messages are removed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A common structure is:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>System instructions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Conversation summary</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Recent unsummarized messages</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Current user message</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure the general direction of the conversation much more efficiently than retaining every original message.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, a summary is more of an interpretation. It omits nuance, simplifies uncertainty, or accidentally turns an assumption into a fact. If we repeatedly summarize previous summaries, it can gradually distort the meaning of the conversation, much like repeatedly copying a photocopy. Therefore, it’s a much better approach to store important facts separately rather than trusting them to be retained in a simple narrative summary.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Structured Entity Extraction</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instead of remembering the conversation as prose, the application can extract specific facts into structured fields. For example:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>{</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “preferred_language”: “TypeScript”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “database”: “PostgreSQL”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “framework”: “Express”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “current_project”: “invoice service”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  “confirmed_decisions”: [</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    “Use optimistic concurrency control”,</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>    “Do not introduce Redis”</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>  ]</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>}</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is more reliable than searching through a long summary when the application needs exact project state.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Structured memory is really useful for the following types of information:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>User preferences</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Names and identifiers</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Confirmed technical decisions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Current tasks</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Workflow status</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Dates and deadlines</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Product configuration</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, structured entity is doesn’t work well for subtle, narrative information that cannot be expressed neatly into predefined fields.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Vector-store-backed Memory</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this approach, a vector store supports semantic retrieval. Instead of putting the entire conversation history into every request, the application divides past conversations into small pieces and creates an embedding for each piece.</span></p><div numerical representation of meaning. This means that texts concerning similar ideas receive similar representations even when they don’t use exactly the same words.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, let’s say the user asks: “Why did we reject Redis for the invoice service?” The memory system searches for past passages semantically related to “Redis,” “invoice service”, and “rejected architecture decisions.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It may retrieve information such as “we decided against Redis because the deployment environment does not provide a managed Redis service, and PostgreSQL advisory locks already cover the required coordination.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Only the retrieved passage is added to the current context. Here’s how the process works roughly:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Store selected pieces of earlier conversations.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Convert those pieces into embeddings.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Convert the new question into an embedding.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Find semantically similar memories.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Filter and rank the candidates.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Insert the best candidates into the model’s prompt.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This doesn’t enlarge the context window. It selects which memories deserve space inside it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, vector retrieval can also sometimes fail. It may retrieve something similar but irrelevant. It can miss a memory because it was phrased strangely. It can also come up with an outdated decision. Metadata such as user ID, project ID, date, and memory type is therefore essential to make sense of this data.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Long-term User Profiles</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A long-term profile stores durable facts that may be useful across many conversations. For example, this could include things like:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The user generally prefers beginner-friendly technical explanations.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Examples should use TypeScript where practical.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Explanations should use complete paragraphs rather than fragmented bullets.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A profile should contain stable preferences, not every passing statement. For example, “I am testing Python today” is probably session information. On the other hand, “I use Python for all data projects” may be a durable preference if repeatedly confirmed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We also need to update profiles. This is because preferences can change over time. Good systems attach timestamps, sources, and sometimes confidence scores to memory entries.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How Cross-session Memory Works</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cross-session memory means that information survives after one chat ends and can influence another chat.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A typical implementation works like this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>During or after a conversation, a memory process identifies potentially durable information.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It stores that information in a user-level, project-level, or organization-level memory store.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A future conversation starts.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The application selects memories relevant to the new conversation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Those memories are inserted into the new conversation’s context.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: is number five. The new model call still needs the remembered information placed into its current context.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we’ve looked at LLM memory in detail. The key takeaways are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Model weights contain general knowledge learned during training.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The context window contains information available for the current response.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Conversation storage holds previous messages.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Long-term memory stores selected facts, preferences, and past events.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The memory manager decides what to retrieve and place on the desk.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It can be said that LLMs, along with the application surrounding them, don’t have the memory of a goldfish. They can process an enormous amount of information at once. But they don’t automatically carry personal experiences from one call to the next.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>What appears to be memory is a carefully constructed system of context reconstruction, summarization, retrieval, and persistent storage. The quality of an LLM application’s memory depends at least as much on the surrounding architecture as it does on the model itself.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" item.title: The Executive Loop
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Executive Loop

Jade Rubick

The job of an executive follows a very simple algorithm: (1) Figure out what needs to happen. (2) Figure out how to make it happen. (3) Make it happen. This is simple, but it’s not easy. In fact, it’s so simple it seems dumb to lay it out. But it’s surprisingly... well, not something people take to automatically.

#Leadership Management
item.description: The Executive Loop

item.title: Confessions Of An Unrepentant Slop Snob
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Confessions Of An Unrepentant Slop Snob

Charity Majors

“So maybe we all just need to be ruthlessly outcome-oriented. Build the best thing we can, as fast as we can. AI is a powerful and versatile tool, so we should use it wherever we can to make our work better and do it faster. Is it really that simple? I had nearly convinced myself that it was, when I noticed how contradictory my own behavior had become.” Charity shares a framework for thinking about when AI involvement is additive or a violation.

#Management CareerGrowth AI
item.description: Confessions Of An Unrepentant Slop Snob

item.title: Why I Stopped Arguing With People
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Why I Stopped Arguing With People

Cong Wang

“Over the years I’ve slowly stopped arguing. Not because I stopped caring about being right, but because I finally understood what an argument actually is, and what it can and cannot do. Here is what changed my mind.”

#Communication Influence
item.description: Why I Stopped Arguing With People

item.title: We Are All Product Engineers Now
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
We Are All Product Engineers Now

Laurie Voss

“This post is an attempt to build on those and make a forecast of where the industry is going in the next 10 years. Making a 10 year forecast of anything is of course a crazy thing to try to do, and especially about the business of software right now. To make it, I had to make two very big assumptions.”

#AI Product IndustryTrends
item.description: We Are All Product Engineers Now

item.title: What Is Happening With Code Reviews?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
What Is Happening With Code Reviews?

Gergely Orosz

“One question haunting the minds of CTOs and heads of engineering whom I’ve been talking with, is how to deal with large quantities of code review which have only been growing now that AI agents generate most code at many tech companies.”

#Management AI CodeReview
item.description: What Is Happening With Code Reviews?

item.title: How Well Do Agents Use Test And Verification Techniques?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How Well Do Agents Use Test And Verification Techniques?

Dan Luu

“Here, we test if simple instructions to agents to use particular techniques or libraries improve implementation correctness, as a kind of test to see how effective agents are when guided by someone with no expertise in testing who's maybe heard that you should apply certain techniques or use certain libraries.”

#AI Testing Agents
item.description: How Well Do Agents Use Test And Verification Techniques?

item.title: The Startup's Postgres Survival Guide
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Startup's Postgres Survival Guide

Alexander Belanger

“Over the past half year or so, I’ve been writing an internal doc for our engineers trying to distill two years of Postgres battles into a somewhat cohesive document. While I love the Postgres manual, I find it’s hard to turn to when shit hits the fan because it’s just so darn comprehensive. I thought this might be useful for others and would appreciate feedback (or other tidbits that you’ve learned running Postgres in production).”

#Guide Database PostgreSQL
item.description: The Startup's Postgres Survival Guide

To evaluate an LLM, we have to measure whether the application continues to behave properly across many situations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“LLM-as-a-Judge” is one part of this evaluation process. It involves using one language model to assess the output generated by another language model. But a judge model isn’t enough on its own. A healthy LLM evaluation system combines several ingredients such as conventional software tests, carefully curated examples, automated checks, model-based judging, human review, and production monitoring.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we are going to look at the process of LLM evaluation in detail. 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>What Does it Mean for an LLM Application to be Healthy?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When can we call an LLM healthy?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The answer is quite simple. An LLM is deemed healthy if it consistently generates useful results while remaining within acceptable limits for accuracy, safety, speed, reliability, and cost. For example, consider a customer-support assistant. We cannot say it is healthy by a single question such as “Did it return the correct output?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We need to consider several different questions:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did it understand what the customer was asking?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Was the answer factually correct based on the company documentation?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did it answer the entire question?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did it follow the required tone and format?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did it avoid inventing policies that do not exist?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did it refuse requests that it should not answer?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did it respond within an acceptable amount of time?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Did the request cost an acceptable amount to process?</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As we can see, these questions are all related to different dimensions of quality, where each dimension is important. We can have an assistant that is friendly and relevant, but it might generate factually incorrect answers. It might be accurate but so verbose that users can’t simply find the answer. It might produce excellent answers but take 30 seconds for every request. Therefore, while evaluating an LLM, we must measure multiple aspects of the system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We also need to differentiate between the health of the LLM and the application. We can’t simply label the model as the source of all problems. The problems can be caused by various sources. For example, we might have an incorrect prompt, missing documents, poor retrieval logic, incorrect tool calls, stale data, or a change in the surrounding code.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Why Ordinary Tests Are Not Sufficient for LLMs?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Traditional software tests usually depend on deterministic behavior. If a function receives a known input, the test expects a specific output. For example:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>Input: add(2, 3)</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Expected output: 5</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This type of test works only because there is one exact correct answer. However, an LLM’s task is different. For example, consider the question “Explain why a password reset link may expire”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One possible response might begin by talking about security. Another response might first explain the expiration period. The way the sentences are written may be totally different even though the underlying answers are correct.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/2a120a73-b629-4fa5-87a0-9d7179a929f8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Three properties make LLM evaluation tricky.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First, the outputs from an LLM are not deterministic. This is because LLMs generate answers using a probability-based approach. We can use the same prompt and model, but the answers may be different. Increasing the model’s temperature only increases the variation. But even if we set a low temperature, it doesn’t make every model and infra combination perfectly repeatable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even an exact string comparison can mark many valid answers as failures. For example, the sentences “The payment was declined because the card expired” and “The card’s expiration date caused the payment to fail” convey the same information.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Second, quality is multidimensional and partly subjective. We can’t have a universally correct level of detail, tone, or organization of the answer. A response appropriate for a developer may simply confuse the customer. A short answer may work well in a support chat. But a longer answer might be more suitable in documentation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This doesn’t imply that quality is impossible to measure. It just means that we need to first define the desired qualities. For example, having a goal like “give a good answer” is too vague to test. A much better option could be something like “Answer the question directly, use only the supplied policy, and explain all required steps”.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Third, the correctness also depends on the context. For example, the answer to “Can this order be refunded?” depends on multiple data points such as order date, product type, account status, region, and current refund policy. A particular response might be correct for one customer and wrong for another.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To evaluate properly, we must therefore include the context available to the model. We must be able to test whether the answer is correct relative to that context.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, traditional testing is still needed for the deterministic parts of an LLM application. For example, things like JSON parsing, permission checks, calculations, database operations, API contracts, and tool execution should continue to rely on the usual unit and integration tests.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Basic Evaluation Loop</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A practical LLM evaluation system is built around a repeated process that works as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Collect representative test cases.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Run the application on those cases.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Inspect the resulting answers with several evaluation methods.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Compare the results with the current production version.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Block or investigate changes that cause an important regression.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Monitor real production traffic for problems that the test set missed.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Add newly discovered failures back into the test set.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 super important. We need to evolve the useful evaluation dataset by adding more examples. Such a dataset grows as real users reveal unexpected questions, ambiguous instructions, document formats, and new ways the system can fail.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Golden Datasets for Repeatable Tests for LLM Behavior</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A golden dataset is a carefully curated collection of possible inputs and information about what a good response to such an input should contain. Think of it as something that plays a role similar to a unit-testing suite. But unlike unit tests, we don’t always check the answers based on exact equality.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, a test case for a refund assistant might contain the following details:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 approach is much more useful than providing one perfectly written reference answer. This is because there may be many reasonable ways to express an answer. The important point is that the LLM makes the correct decision while following the stated constraints.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We should create a strong golden dataset with more than just easy and ordinary requests. It should ideally include the following:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Common requests that represent most real traffic.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Important cases where an incorrect answer would cause significant harm.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Ambiguous questions that require clarification.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Questions for which the answer is absent from the supplied information.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Malicious or irrelevant instructions embedded inside retrieved documents.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Very short, very long, poorly written, and multilingual inputs where relevant.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Previous production failures.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Boundary cases, such as a return made exactly on the final allowed day.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We should also divide the dataset into groups. A development set can be used while prompts are in the improvement phase. However, a separate holdout set should remain less visible during the development phase. Otherwise, the prompt may gradually be tailored to known examples without becoming better for real users.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We should not consider golden datasets as static input-output pairs. Depending on the application, a test case may contain an input, source documents, expected facts, forbidden claims, acceptable tool calls, a scoring rubric, and an optional reference response.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Automated Metrics: Fast but Limited Checks</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Despite the non-deterministic nature, automated metrics are also useful in testing LLMs. However, automated metrics use code rather than another person or model to inspect an answer. They are also cheap, fast, and repeatable. Therefore, they are useful for running large numbers of tests.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Exact match checks help where the output has to precisely match an expected value. It works well for constrained extraction tasks such as returning a country code, classification label, or database identifier. But it works poorly for open-ended natural-language answers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Regular expressions and schema validators help check whether an output follows a required structure. For example, an application may require valid JSON containing fields such as customer_id, issue_type, and priority. In such a case, a validator can reliably check whether those fields exist and whether their values use the expected types.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Programmatic checks can help verify URLs, citations, numerical ranges, required phrases, banned phrases, word limits, or whether specific product IDs exist in a database.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) and ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) compare the words or word sequences in a generated answer with those in a reference answer. BLEU became popular for machine translation, while ROUGE has often been used for summarization. They can be useful for certain large-scale comparisons. But they mainly deal with measuring textual overlap. We can have a response with a different arrangement of words that still preserves the meaning.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Other semantic similarity metrics compare the meanings of responses through embeddings or specialized evaluation models. These metrics are more flexible than word overlap, but we still cannot treat similarity the same as correctness. An incorrect answer about the right subject can still be semantically similar to the reference answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The main limitation is that automated metrics generally measure a narrow, observable property. They should be used for things that code can check reliably.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>What Does LLM-as-a-Judge Mean?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LLM-as-a-Judge involves sending one language model’s answer to another language model and asking that model to evaluate it based on specific criteria.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: href="https://substack.com/redirect/30440944-c98d-4497-92b4-b5cae01b94be?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction:
