consider an RAG assistant that answers a question using retrieved company documents. The judge may receive:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The original question.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The documents supplied to the assistant.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The assistant’s answer.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The evaluation rubric.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An optional reference answer.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The judge LLM can then assess qualities such as relevance, factual support, completeness, clarity, and compliance with instructions. For reference, a simplified judge prompt might say:</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background: rgb(255,255,255);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 12px;box-sizing: border-box;white-space: pre-wrap;font-family: monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 24px;font-weight: 500;background-color: #fff;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>Evaluate the response using only the supplied policy.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Score each category from 1 to 5:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Accuracy:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Does every factual claim agree with the policy?</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Completeness:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Does the response answer every part of the question?</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Relevance:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Does it remain focused on the customer’s request?</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Instruction compliance:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Does it avoid making promises not supported by the policy?</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Return JSON with the scores, a short explanation, and the exact unsupported claims, if any.</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We can store the output from the judge model to compare with previous evaluation runs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This approach is far more flexible than exact matching because the judge can recognize that differently worded responses express the same idea. It can also identify subtle failures such as answering only half of a question or introducing a claim that might not be present in the evidence.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Different Ways a Judge Model Can Evaluate an Answer</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are several common methods for judging an answer. Let us look at each of them in detail.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Point-based Scoring</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this approach, the judge model assigns scores such as 1 to 5 for different quality dimensions. This results in numbers that are easier to track over time as we refine the model under testing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The main drawback of this approach is that the meaning of a score may be inconsistent. We need to define every score and its rubric properly.  For example, consider the following scores:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>5: Every factual claim is supported by the provided documents.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>4: The main answer is supported, with one insignificant unsupported detail.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>3: The answer is mostly correct but contains a meaningful unsupported claim.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>2: Several important claims are unsupported or incorrect.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>1: The central conclusion contradicts the documents.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Pass or Fail Classification</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The judge model can also decide whether an output meets a minimum standard. We can use it for deployment gates, especially when the requirement is crystal clear. For example, “the answer must not contradict policy, expose personal information, or produce invalid instructions.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A pass-or-fail result is simple, but it hides smaller changes. A score can decline from excellent to barely acceptable without crossing the failure boundary.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Pairwise Comparison</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this method, the judge model receives two answers and decides which one is better. For example, it may compare the response from the current production prompt with the response from a proposed prompt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pairwise comparison is often easier than assigning an absolute score. We can decide whether answer A is more useful than answer B more consistently than deciding whether one answer deserves a score of 3 or 4 out of 5.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To make this method better, the order of the answers should sometimes be reversed. Judge models can have a position bias and may start favoring whichever response appears first or second.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Error Identification</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instead of merely producing a score, the judge model can also identify specific problems.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The judge model can list unsupported claims, unanswered parts of the question, irrelevant sections, or violated instructions. This is quite useful during the development phase because it explains why a score has changed from one value to another.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Human Evaluation and Calibration</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Despite all the advancements in testing, the ultimate test of a model’s ability depends on human evaluation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Human evaluation involves people reviewing model outputs using the same rubric. This is why domain experts are really important when the correctness of an answer depends on legal, medical, financial, scientific, or company-specific knowledge.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, since humans are expensive and slow, they cannot inspect every answer. Their best role is often to calibrate things. To make this work, human reviewers rate a representative sample. The results are compared with the ratings of a judge LLM.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, let’s say experts mark 100 answers as pass or fail. The same answers are evaluated by the judge model. The exercise reveals how often the judge agrees with the experts, which types of failure it misses, and whether its passing threshold needs adjustment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Human reviewers can also disagree with one another. This usually means that the rubric is a little ambiguous or that the task is genuinely subjective. We should, therefore, measure reviewer agreement before treating human scores as a perfect reference point.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Human evaluation for LLMs remains highly important for:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Creating and validating the first rubric.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Reviewing high-risk failures.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Evaluating new kinds of requests.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Checking whether automated scores reflect real usefulness.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Investigating disagreement between different evaluators.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Periodically auditing the judge for drift.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Evaluation Stack</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Having gone through all the methods of LLM evaluation, we can now look at the overall evaluation stack.</span></p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We should understand this proposed evaluation stack as a set of complementary layers rather than a strict ladder where one layer replaces another.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>At the bottom are conventional software tests. These are used to verify deterministic components such as permissions, tool schemas, database writes, and calculations.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Golden datasets provide repeatable scenarios on which the entire LLM application can be tested.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Automated checks inspect properties that can be measured reliably, including valid JSON, required fields, exact extracted values, citation structure, and latency.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>LLM judges evaluate qualities that require the model to interpret meaning. We can use it to assess whether an answer is relevant, complete, supported by evidence, and compliant with a detailed rubric.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Human reviewers calibrate the judge and assess cases where the consequences or subjectivity are too great to rely entirely on automation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Production monitoring completes the stack. A test set can never anticipate every real request, so production signals are needed to reveal emerging failures.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We should not treat LLM evaluation as a search for a perfect accuracy number. It is a system for building confidence in a model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Golden datasets make critical situations repeatable. Automated metrics quickly check narrow and objective properties. LLM judges assess meaning according to a rubric. Human reviewers calibrate those judges and handle difficult decisions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The most reliable question is therefore not simply, “Is the model healthy?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It is the idea that across the situations that matter, does the complete application stay accurate, useful, safe, reliable, fast, and affordable? Also, is there enough evidence to detect when that changes?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>This is the real purpose of LLM evaluation.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><table item.title: How to name things
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to name things

Koleman Nix

11 minutes by Koleman Nix Koleman says that good naming is one of the most important skills in software, because vague language usually means vague thinking. Names carry meaning for teammates, future readers, and AI tools alike, so choosing them well is an act of empathy. Rather than following rigid rules, good naming means studying the essence of a thing, looking at how nearby concepts relate, and asking how a reader will understand the name in context. A bad name often signals a deeper design problem worth fixing. Revel is hiring. Build the next generation of software for
item.description: How to name things

item.title: A faster way to convert a timestamp
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
A faster way to convert a timestamp

Ben Joffe

7 minutes by Ben Joffe Most datetime libraries compute hours, minutes, and seconds using a chain of division steps where each result depends on the previous one, making parallelisation impossible. By reordering the calculations to break this dependency chain, and using fixed-point multiplication tricks instead of division, you can cut the process from around 16 CPU steps down to just two multiplications.
item.description: A faster way to convert a timestamp

item.title: Good APIs age slowly
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Good APIs age slowly

Yusuf Aytas

6 minutes by Yusuf Aytas APIs that look elegant at first often cause the most trouble later. The real test is how an API holds up after different teams use it, requirements shift, and people rely on behavior that was never meant to be a promise. Yusuf points out that most problems come down to boundaries: once something is visible, people build on it, whether you intended that or not. His advice: Expose as little as possible, because adding later is easy, but removing is painful.
item.description: Good APIs age slowly

item.title: A coding agent is six functions in a trenchcoat
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
A coding agent is six functions in a trenchcoat

Hadley Wickham

8 minutes by Hadley Wickham Coding agents like Claude Code and Cursor work by giving an AI model tools to read, write, search, and edit files, plus run shell commands. You can build a basic version with just three functions in around 30 lines of code. Adding targeted file editing makes the agent faster and cheaper, since the model only rewrites changed lines rather than entire files. Safety matters too, as path checks and scoped tools prevent the agent from accessing files outside the project.
item.description: A coding agent is six functions in a trenchcoat

item.title: How well do agents use test and verification techniques?
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How well do agents use test and verification techniques?

about 1 hour by Dan Luu AI coding agents mostly fail to use testing tools and techniques effectively, even when explicitly told to. Telling agents to use property-based testing, formal methods, or TDD changes their surface behavior but rarely changes the underlying quality of tests. Default instructions with no testing guidance outperformed most specific approaches, because specific instructions mostly just caused agents to do useless work inside unfamiliar frameworks. Simple, targeted nudges away from bad defaults worked better than detailed skill documents or named techniques.
item.description: How well do agents use test and verification techniques?

item.title: Less known LINQ methods
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Less known LINQ methods

Ricardo Peres

LINQ has many useful extension methods that developers often overlook. Methods like Chunk, CountBy, and AggregateBy help with grouping and reducing data, while Append, Prepend, and Index simplify common list operations. Others like LeftJoin, FullJoin, and ToLookup handle more complex data relationships. As Ricardo points out, each method has a clear purpose and can replace manual, error-prone code.
item.description: Less known LINQ methods

item.title: Reading a profiler trace without guessing
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Reading a profiler trace without guessing

Bart Wullems

The Azure Monitor Profiler trace explorer has two views of call stack data: a flame graph and a profile tree. Start with the Hot path feature, which jumps straight to the likely bottleneck. The labels on hot nodes tell you what kind of problem you have, such as CPU cost, lock contention, or async waiting, and each points to a different fix. Code Optimizations can analyze profiler traces automatically and surface bottlenecks without you opening a trace at all.
item.description: Reading a profiler trace without guessing

item.title: ASP.NET Core circuit breaker pattern explained
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
ASP.NET Core circuit breaker pattern explained

Yohan Malshika

When one service in your app fails, repeated calls to it can slow everything down and crash your whole system. The circuit breaker pattern fixes this by stopping calls to a failing service before the damage spreads. It works like an electrical circuit breaker, cutting the connection when something goes wrong and retrying later. This keeps your ASP.NET Core app stable even when outside services go down.
item.description: ASP.NET Core circuit breaker pattern explained

item.title: The interesting stuff in .NET 11
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The interesting stuff in .NET 11

DeeDee Walsh

.NET 11 focuses on practical improvements that make real-world software easier to run and maintain. It improves Linux container support, crash reporting, process management, JSON modeling, and CI/CD performance. It also adds better kiosk support for Windows Forms. Overall, the release focuses less on flashy features and more on reliability, performance, security, and smoother development for enterprise and production systems.
item.description: The interesting stuff in .NET 11

item.title: Finding hidden latency across a distributed .NET application
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Finding hidden latency across a distributed .NET application

Justin Yoo

A slow distributed app can hide its bottleneck across many processes. Profiling only the wrong process, like the frontend when the backend is slow, gives a clean bill of health while the real problem stays hidden. Justin shows how to isolate the right process, capture its CPU activity, and recognize when CPU data alone is not enough. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Finding hidden latency across a distributed .NET application

Here’s why that happens.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">What git revert actually does: Unlike reset, a revert doesn’t rewrite history. Instead, it creates a new commit that undoes the changes from an earlier one. This keeps your history clean, traceable, and safe for shared branches.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Why revert conflicts happen: Conflicts appear when a later commit changed the same lines as the commit you’re trying to undo.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Example in the diagram:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Commit C2 added a feature</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Commit C3 changed those same lines</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Reverting C2 now collides with changes from C3</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Git can’t know which version is correct, so a revert conflict is triggered.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to resolve it:</span><br><span>1. Run git revert C2</span><br><span>2. Git pauses when it hits the conflict</span><br><span>3. You manually fix the file</span><br><span>4. Stage it</span><br><span>5. Continue the revert</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Git then creates a new commit that cleanly undoes C2 while keeping C3 intact.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Over to you: Have you ever hit a revert conflict at the worst possible moment? encryption often get explained together, but they solve very different problems.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Symmetric encryption uses a single shared key. The same key encrypts and decrypts the data. It’s fast, efficient, and ideal for large amounts of data. That’s why it’s used for things like encrypting files, database records, and message payloads.</span><br><br><span>The catch is key distribution, both parties must already have the secret, and sharing it securely is hard.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair. A public key that can be shared with anyone, and a private key that stays secret. Data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the private key.</span><br><br><span>This removes the need for secure key sharing upfront, but it comes at a cost. It’s slower and computationally expensive, which makes it impractical for encrypting large payloads.</span><br><br><span>That’s why asymmetric encryption is usually used for identity, authentication, and key exchange, not bulk data.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Over to you: What’s the most common misunderstanding you’ve rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Session Persistence: Load Balancers ensure that all requests from a user hit the 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Scalability: Load Balancers facilitate horizontal scaling 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">DDoS Mitigation: Load Balancers can help mitigate the impact of DDoS attacks by rate limiting requests or distributing them rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Thunder herd problem</span><br><span>This happens when a large number of keys in the cache expire at the same time. Then the query requests directly hit the database, which overloads the database.</span><br><br><span>There are two ways to mitigate this issue: one is to avoid setting the same expiry time for the keys, adding a random number in the configuration; the other is to allow only the core business data to hit the database and prevent non-core data to access the database until the cache is back up.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cache penetration</span><br><span>This happens when the key doesn’t exist in the cache or the database. The application cannot retrieve relevant data from the database to update the cache. This problem creates a lot of pressure on both the cache and the database.</span><br><br><span>To solve this, there are two suggestions. One is to cache a null value for non-existent keys, avoiding hitting the database. The other is to use a bloom filter to check the key existence first, and if the key doesn’t exist, we can avoid hitting the database.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cache breakdown</span><br><span>This is similar to the thunder herd problem. It happens when a hot key expires. A large number of requests hit the database.</span><br><br><span>Since the hot keys take up 80% of the queries, we do not set an expiration time for them.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cache crash</span><br><span>This happens when the cache is down and all the requests go to the database.</span><br><br><span>There are two ways to solve this problem. One is to set up a circuit breaker, and when the cache is down, the application services cannot visit the cache or the database. The other is to set up a cluster for the cache to improve cache availability.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Over to you: Have you met any of these issues in production?</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">Launching ByteByteGo Live</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Most online courses never get finished (~4% completion). item.title: How To Grow Past Senior Engineer
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How To Grow Past Senior Engineer

Gregor Ojstersek

In this article, you can expect 4 actionable pieces of advice on making a move to your next step and make a convincing proposal to increase your chances. I’ll cover: (1) Talking to your manager. (2) Keeping a brag list of all the wins that you achieve. (3) Become the go-to person for a specific project, specific technology, or specific domain. (4) Propose an impactful improvement to the codebase and own the implementation.

#CareerGrowth Staff+
item.description: How To Grow Past Senior Engineer

item.title: The Semmelweis Reflex
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Semmelweis Reflex

Mike Fisher

“This week, think back to the last time a report, a survey, a customer complaint or a colleague’s warning challenged one of your own decisions. Yours, not the organization’s. Ask what you did with it, and then ask what happened to the person who carried it in. Did the evidence get a fair hearing, or did a reasonable-sounding explanation make it easier to set aside?“

#Leadership DecisionMaking Feedback
item.description: The Semmelweis Reflex

item.title: 5 Things World-Class Engineers Do That You Don't
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
5 Things World-Class Engineers Do That You Don't

Steve Huynh

“After participating in many such conversations, both through my podcast and during my time at Amazon, I have recognized a handful of patterns that have held over the decades and across different companies. What follows is my running list of those patterns, the ones that keep surfacing whenever I sit down with someone elite. There are five of them, and I explain the gap between what they do and where most other people stop.”

#CareerGrowth
item.description: 5 Things World-Class Engineers Do That You Don't

item.title: Wisdom Isn’t Hard To Find, It’s Hard To Receive
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Wisdom Isn’t Hard To Find, It’s Hard To Receive

Yew Jin Lim

"Wisdom is the ability to act on a truth before experience makes it obvious. That’s different from intelligence. Intelligence helps you figure things out for yourself while wisdom tells you which lessons you don’t need to insist on learning yourself.”

#Leadership CareerGrowth
item.description: Wisdom Isn’t Hard To Find, It’s Hard To Receive

item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>

The End Of Code Review? Or An Opportunity To Rethink It?

Christian Kästner

“Implicit in this discussion is often the assumption that our prior code review practices were a gold standard, something to save or something to mourn. But is that really the case?”

#IndustryTrends AI CodeReview
item.description: The End Of Code Review? Or An Opportunity To Rethink It?

item.title: How One Connection Kills A Database
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How One Connection Kills A Database

Simeon Griggs

“Years ago at GitHub, this was a question Sam Lambert would ask in interviews. The solution involved a downed database that started with a MySQL schema change needing an exclusive lock on a table, but it couldn't get one. Another session had already touched that table and never committed. That open transaction blocked the schema change.”

#CaseStudy Debugging Database
item.description: How One Connection Kills A Database

New trend of CPU shortages</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I was at dinner with a bunch of CTOs and Head of Infrastructure folks recently, and from the conversation it was clear that many companies are struggling to source CPUs in the current climate, and are coming to terms with the end of juicy discounts from cloud providers for machines in the new era of surging demand fueled by AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The ‘memory crisis’ afflicting sectors like video gaming is well established and has been extensively covered in terms of shortages of GPUs, but now it seems like things are just as hard for businesses in need of CPUs from cloud providers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In a sign of how things are changing, the disappearance of CPU spot pricing was mentioned at the table. Customers used to be able to pay up to 90% less than the standard price for CPUs, as cloud providers slashed CPU prices for machines that were lying dormant and unused. But that’s no longer the case. It seems that spot pricing has vanished because there’s no longer any lack of demand for CPUs – quite the opposite.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I was surprised, but a lot of people chimed in; apparently, it’s now nearly impossible to get CPUs on spot instances without long-running connections with cloud providers. Also, reserving specific CPUs now needs to be done months in advance, and cloud providers will even turn down certain reservations because they don’t have enough CPUs or the right type of CPUs.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Even big players struggle to reserve CPUs</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I have asked turbopuffer CEO Simon Eskildsen about their experience of CPU availability in the cloud, since turbopuffer, as a product, runs on CPUs, not GPUs. They operate in AWS, GCP, and Azure, so I asked how easy it is to get CPUs these days. Simon’s response:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>Getting CPUs is not easy anymore. </span></strong><span>As Reinforcement Learning (RL) is becoming a large amount of the workloads: RL needs a lot of CPUs. So the labs are sucking up a lot of CPUs. During RL, they need to teach the models how to do things, like searching, and then they need the model to run software, which then takes CPUs to run.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Then, outside of RL, agents need to do all kinds of very general purpose things on a CPU. So as the demand curve is shifting to general purpose agents, CPU demand is also going up.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Even the big companies are fighting each other for the right to get the CPU allocations. </span></strong><span>I would assume that it gets a lot worse before it gets better on the CPU side.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I was able to confirm what Simon said about larger companies struggling; a VP of Engineering at a large inference provider told me they are at the limit on how much GPU and CPU capacity they can buy from their cloud providers. They have cash to spend and want to rent more capacity, and are willing to accept the longest leases. Despite that, cloud providers tell them no more is available!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>AI hogging CPUs</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn Lesse, Head of Platform Engineering for Claude Platform, has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce7ffe9e-e10d-46af-9b92-9ec123b7f8f2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>written about</span></a><span> the reasons for the massive CPU demand increase:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“In the past few years, AI-fueled demand has skyrocketed, and these few companies suddenly needed multiple years and tens of billions of dollars to actually add enough capacity. We ended up with 3 separate bottlenecks in factory capacity that AI is exacerbating. At TSMC, GPUs are competing with CPUs (and with Apple, Qualcomm, and Broadcom) for production lines. And at SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron, HBM [High Bandwidth Memory] is competing with regular DRAM for wafers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What we’ve ended up with is CPUs getting squeezed from both sides. AMD doesn’t own fabs [semiconductor fabrication plants], so its CPUs need to come out of TSMC’s constrained allocation. Intel does own fabs, but it’s been working through yield problems and is now pulling some of its capacity from PC chips in order to make more server chips. And CPUs need DRAM which has gotten more expensive because memory production has shifted toward HBM. Analysts are expecting CPU supply to add more comfortable headroom before memory does, but their expectation is that it’s still going to be multiple quarters away.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI-fueled demand does increase CPU load, as shown in this graph from Uber, displaying the growth in agent requests over the past six months:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce86bafe-fb94-4a5b-b5e7-3a7cdd2b9071?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Ninefold increase in agentic requests over six months. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/399b9a25-afba-4758-935f-514b7cd5bcc6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Uber</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Increasingly, “agent requests” not only generate code which is inference-heavy – and therefore needs GPUs – but they also run tools that compile the code, run tests, run linters, and all of this is CPU-heavy. At companies like Uber, Ramp, and others, AI agents no longer run on the dev’s local machine, but on a dedicated instance in the cloud. So, the companies reserve more CPUs on their respective cloud providers for agentic workloads. </span><em><span>We recently covered </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/da121b4c-8140-4e5e-984e-00a4312e2858?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>how Ramp built and runs its cloud agent, Inspect.</span></a></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Basically, the problem is:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>AI applications use more and more CPUs, </span></strong><span>thanks to agents running a lot more software. AI data centers used to have a ratio of 1 CPU to 8 GPUs. Now the ratio is more 1:4, and it could shrink to 1:1.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Companies that can manufacture more CPUs are busy on other hardware. </span></strong><span>TSMC is busy producing GPUs, which might be more profitable than CPUs. Meanwhile, CPUs also need DRAM, but DRAM manufacturers (SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron) are instead producing high-bandwidth memory (HBM) because it’s more profitable. This is why </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/10bb462f-a235-4156-88fd-bd1263e71876?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>memory prices are spiking</span></a><span>; even Big Tech is unable to buy RAM, as previously covered.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>To secure CPUs, it’s necessary to do capacity planning up to 12 months in advance. </span></strong><span>Katelyn says that server orders are being fulfilled in ~six months, instead of 1-2 weeks’ time as previously, and that prices are up by between 10-20%. So, it’s probably time for capacity planning. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce7ffe9e-e10d-46af-9b92-9ec123b7f8f2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Katelyn</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Most of us have never capacity-planned CPUs. We planned databases, we maybe planned accelerators if we needed them, and we autoscaled on-demand into CPU capacity as much as our budgets allowed us to. But general purpose compute is now something many teams will need to commit to ahead of time, which means you should probably start to forecast and plan around it. If you’re operating at scale, there are some things to spend your energy on.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Using existing CPUs more efficiently is something to do, as of now. </span></strong><span>The CPU capacity shortage won’t go away, and any new CPU allocations requested could take months to turn up. So, what can we do if new capacity lags? One option is utilizing current resources more efficiently!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is a great time to review and to establish now which services are CPU-intensive, and whether or not they </span><em><span>need</span></em><span> to be. Also check on services which are utilizing little CPU: can they run on fewer nodes, so that some CPU capacity can be allocated to services that need it more?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The best time to secure more CPU capacity is most certainly </span></strong><em><strong><span>right now</span></strong></em><strong><span>. </span></strong><span>I’m hearing rumors that certain cloud regions no longer accept new tenants because all CPU capacity is leased, or negotiations elsewhere are difficult. I’m also hearing that customers are already paying </span><em><span>today</span></em><span> to reserve capacity that will only come online in data centers from December. This seems predatory by providers, but demand is so high that this is how they likely prioritize new capacity allocation – </span><em><span>while</span></em><span> </span><em><span>earning much higher profits than usual.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If your company has dynamic workloads, and you’ve used spot instances in the past, now could be a good time to allocate fixed capacity – even if it’s more expensive. If you expect meaningful growth, doing so now might mean having options at some cloud providers or in some regions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It seems like this issue has spread everywhere as a corollary of widespread AI adoption. There’s a GPU shortage, memory shortage, and now a growing CPU shortage as well. Back at the end of last year, there was even an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/12971a90-6bc5-4cd0-9a08-6c623c831414?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>hard drive shortage</span></a><span>. </span><em><span>The only compute primitive not in short supply seems to be networking!</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>2. Growth dream ends for more COVID-era unicorns</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Bending Spoons continues its shopping spree of buying up well-known VC-funded businesses which are desperate to sell, possibly because growth has dried up. Today, the company </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0685c470-33fc-465a-b67f-4cc7a34bc5b8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>announced</span></a><span> its purchase of digital whiteboard startup </span><strong><span>Miro</span></strong><span> for $1.35B. Miro raised a total of $476M in funding, and was valued at a whopping $17.5B in 2022. The acquisition price being higher than what Miro raised, suggests that investors and equity holders should make money on the acquisition.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It comes after Bending Spoons </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/898dc03b-fd9b-4f02-baea-5f2a1fca2d06?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>bought</span></a><span> </span><strong><span>Airtable</span></strong><span> for $1.2B recently – a company that raised $1.4B in funding and was valued at $11B in 2021 during the pandemic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These days, Miro and Airtable likely have flat or sluggish revenue growth and no path to tap into “AI growth”. They depend on sales of their software to enterprises, but enterprise sales are expensive! Also, with AI agents spreading, it’s not clear how much moat that businesses like theirs will have against “AI-native” products, looking ahead.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the circumstances, the founders likely made a calculated decision that it is better to sell now for as much as possible than to run a stagnating business with apparently shrinking prospects in the longer term.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Miro was founded in 2011 and Airtable a year later. Miro became the global leader in the digital whiteboard market, while Airtable offered a fresh alternative to online spreadsheets. Both remain healthy businesses, generating well over $100M in revenue. But in around 2021-2022, each decided to raise money at massive valuations by riding the pandemic-era wave of demand for digital products, which exploded at the time. Back in 2022, I was skeptical these companies could live up to such high valuations when external conditions settled back to ‘normal’:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" 2022</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Hopefully, early employees at both companies still see payouts after the acquisitions by Bending Spoons. The new owner usually takes all operations in-house, lets go of most staff, and isn’t shy about drastically increasing prices in order to maximize revenue. It’s a well-worn strategy, and both Airtable and Miro founders sold to a buyer with a reputation for making job cuts - but which also pays in cash more than any private equity company would.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>3. Industry Pulse</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Overtime at Google to get Borg working on SpaceX’s data centers</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Google </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a371667-592d-43fb-ab6d-e6ae0b64ff11?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>is paying</span></a><span> SpaceX $920M per month to rent compute in SpaceX’s data centers, but utilizing all this expensive compute is causing problems inside the search giant – because of Borg!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/598aaaa1-bc1f-4ebe-9022-089cd6810412?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Borg</span></a><span> is the system that manages Google’s physical infrastructure. It’s a “Kubernetes, but before Kubernetes” type of software. Kubernetes was created based on learnings from Borg.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>From talking with current Google engineers, we’ve learnt that Borg makes assumptions on data center internals like networking and physical layout that are true for all Google data centers. The big issue is that these assumptions are wrong for SpaceX data centers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As a result, engineers are struggling to get Borg to run on SpaceX’s infrastructure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>So, the Borg team is currently running on a ‘996’ working schedule</span></strong><span> (996 meaning 9am - 9pm, six days a week) because every day that Borg cannot run on SpaceX infra costs Google around $30M in infrastructure losses (given the monthly $920M cost). Google no longer has lots of long-tenured engineers who are deeply familiar with Borg internals.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m hearing that it’s not all complaints from engineers about this, and that many enjoy taking on a “proper” infrastructure challenge, especially since Borg was supposed to have ‘solved’ infrastructure at Google. Well, it now needs to do it again, as running on non-Google infra is the new baseline at a time when compute capacity is constrained.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, the clock is ticking: Google will have to pay a massive amount to SpaceX, whether or not they can make Borg compatible with SpaceX data centers!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Spotify cuts Claude Code token usage by 90%</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Streaming platform Spotify has vastly </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a406cf6-9ffb-42f7-b117-663c1e483f79?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>reduced</span></a><span> its Claude Code token usage by 90%. Here’s how they did it:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Do not use Claude for I/O work: </span></strong><span>much of what Claude Code does is reading and writing files, so why use an expensive model like Claude for this? Instead, Spotify has replaced it with a cheap model like Gemini 2.5 Flash for more basic tasks</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Use Claude only for reasoning: </span></strong><span>Claude is an expensive, capable model, which Spotify keeps in reserve for the most complex tasks that require reasoning</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Use a router to route to Claude or a cheaper alternative: </span></strong><span>Spotify created a Claude Code plugin called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ed3c9ec9-4e88-47d5-a403-df5bbfa1d6a6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>shunt</span></a><span> which routes I/O work to cheaper models</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This work by Spotify fits into a wider trend of token cost-saving efforts by tech companies, which </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aebe2957-2dcf-42c9-b7f5-109b1b2c9ae4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>we covered last week</span></a><span>. The idea is pretty simple: don’t use expensive frontier models for work that is simple, and doesn’t require (or benefit from) the capabilities of frontier models.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple normal;"><span>OpenAI’s agents go rogue again</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Reuters </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6858431e-28ca-4243-9033-774f8cea54f2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>reports</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents, according to ​new research published Friday, and two people familiar with the matter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI officials learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it under wraps as executives grappled with the fallout from ‌the July breach of the open source repository Hugging Face, the people said.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This incident happened before OpenAI’s model-in-training went rogue and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8d4f3510-8cc9-4c13-b817-28d677e35da8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>hacked Hugging Face</span></a><span>, back in July.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Whatever sandbox OpenAI is using for its AI training looks like it’s pretty leaky. Likewise, whatever monitoring they use to track agent actions is clearly not granular enough. Finally, the fact that OpenAI kept this incident under wraps because of fears about how it would look is concerning.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s no transparency on how AI labs train their AI agents or how they monitor them, and given that agents have a tendency to want to hack services and websites, it is not defensible for OpenAI to pretend that nothing happened. The company has pledged to do better at tracking and monitoring its models, Reuters reports.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>And it’s not just OpenAI: it’s also Anthropic. </span></strong><span>OpenAI’s chief competitor </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9765f846-8282-493b-99e8-ced61e40159f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>published reports</span></a><span> yesterday of their own model hacked external systems during a cyber evaluation. And Anthropic is supposedly the lab which was founded to focus on safety: and yet, they also cannot safely train or evaluate their own models!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If a person hacks into a website and is detected, they could well face criminal charges. When an autonomous AI agent does the same, it raises questions: who is the responsible party and who’s liable? Another point is how the law will decide in cases like this latest one in Germany – it’s surely just a matter of time.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>4. Do engineers lose touch when AI handles incidents?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/88b70b7b-38b4-449a-98e6-9d6fdf2dbc61?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>thoughtful post</span></a><span> has been published about what it means when AI starts “taking over” incident response duties. Software engineer Sylvain Kalache, who works at incident management startup, Rootly, wrote (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The better these tools become at resolving routine incidents, the less practice human responders will get. And when an ambiguous, high-severity incident comes in that automation cannot solve, responding engineers will be in trouble.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The problem is that routine incidents are also how responders “safely” develop an intuition for how their systems behave and fail. When AI runs into a hard, never-seen-before incident it cannot solve, engineers will have to take over with less practice than they would have had before.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Human-factors researcher Lisanne Bainbridge described this paradox in her famous 1983 paper, The Ironies of Automation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>She explained that automation reduces operators’ opportunities to practice routine work while leaving them responsible for new and abnormal situations.</span></strong><span> She argues that, therefore, operators need to be more skilled and receive even more training than before automation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the years to come, I predict that the average MTTR [Mean Time to Resolve] for most incidents will go down – thanks to AI-assisted incident response – but that the resolution time will shoot up for complex incidents because incident responders lost touch with their system and are struggling to investigate.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Sylvain uses the aviation industry as an example, where pilots regularly rehearse responses to unlikely emergency situations – and must do so every six months!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>From my time at Uber, I recall the SRE team organized outage drills and these exercises were surprisingly useful. </span></strong><span>They simulated an outage to which we needed to respond by confirming whether it was an outage, then deciding on mitigation, communication, and how to resolve it. Afterward, we reviewed our actions and compared them to what should have been expected.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I did this exercise, and it was </span><em><span>very</span></em><span> useful, even though I knew it was staged. I felt a similar rush as during a real incident. It revealed that some things were not great in our response: we were missing runbooks on how to do routine things, we did not clarify who would communicate and where, and our debugging tooling was missing a few tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Sylvain himself argues that the software industry also needs incident simulators, and that they should become part of oncall readiness. anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>Imagine a simple scenario where an e-commerce web application calls an API endpoint that returns information about a customer order.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the application level, this looks like a pretty simple operation. But a lot is happening under the hood. First, the client queries the DNS for the IP address linked to the API endpoint. DNS might return the address of a load balancer rather than the address of a specific application server. The operating system then determines how packets should be sent to that IP address. It might choose to send them through the local network, an internet service provider (ISP), or several other routers. The ultimate goal is for the data packets to reach the destination network.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure protocol used for this is HTTP. However, before HTTP can send the request, the client usually needs to establish some form of connection with the destination server.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With traditional HTTPS, this means setting up a TCP connection. In this type of connection, the client and server perform a handshake by exchanging some initial packets so that both sides know a connection has been established. The client and server then perform a TLS handshake. Only after this can the HTTP request be sent securely. A load balancer receives it, selects a healthy application instance, and forwards the request. The application performs its work and sends the response back through the same path.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All of this falls under the realm of networking.
